Tprep​(wcat,m)+η⁡(2​n+8)≤TSEC​(n).T_{\mathrm{prep}}(w_{\mathrm{cat}},m)+\eta(2n+8)\leq T_{\mathrm{SEC}}(n). (6)

Under this condition, proposition 2 gives r=1r=1 for every measurement, for kk cat-state registers in total.

The concrete Q102 and Q66 register counts used in the component footprints are calculated in Sec. E.1.

XII.3.2 Reusing Cat States

The elliptic-curve circuit’s limited global logical-measurement parallelism leaves many cat-state resources idle for long periods of time under the default Walking Cat architecture’s per-code-block cat-state allocation policy. This motivates provisioning only enough cat states to meet the circuit’s peak measurement parallelism, then transporting and reusing them across the device as needed. The basic unit of reuse is the complete set of resources needed to pipeline one logical measurement around the local loop: rr weight-wcatw_{\mathrm{cat}} cat-state registers, with rr given by proposition 2, together with one bank of wcatw_{\mathrm{cat}} verification ancillas for successive cat-state preparations. We call this a cat-state bundle.

For the global routing analysis, we arrange the targets of each of the kk parallel logical measurements into an ordered stream. Each stream is served by a pool of reusable cat-state bundles that may travel between code blocks. We ask how many bundles each stream needs to avoid delaying logical measurements.

The registers within each bundle allow one cat state to be prepared and verified while another is consumed, as in proposition 2; the ancilla bank travels with the registers so that the bundle can operate beside any memory block. Upon arrival at the destination code block, the bundle docks at one of the cat-state factories along the target block’s edge and undergoes the preparation and verification procedure of Sec. XII.3.1. At least one bundle remains beside the active block throughout its logical measurement, but the bundle that begins the protocol need not be the one that finishes it. The bundles assigned to each measurement stream follow a handoff schedule, illustrated for two bundles in Fig. 9. The lookahead bundle begins the measurement at the current target while the trailing bundle travels to that same block and is prepared and verified there. The trailing bundle then takes over the ongoing measurement, releasing the lookahead bundle to advance to the following target. Repeating this handoff moves the bundles through the ordered stream of logical measurements.

Consider MM memory blocks packed in an RR-by-CC rectangle, where M≤R​CM\leq RC and unused positions, if any, are left empty. As above, each block occupies a 44-by-nn rectangle. We leave one additional horizontal routing row between neighboring block rows. The maximum Manhattan distance between corresponding ports of two memory blocks is therefore

Dmax​(R,C,n)=n⁡(C−1)+5​(R−1)D_{\max}(R,C,n)=n(C-1)+5(R-1) (7)

transport steps. Let TLMT_{\mathrm{LM}} be the duration in POCs of the shortest logical measurement in the workload.

Proposition 3.

Let L=η​Dmax​(R,C,n)+Tprep​(wcat,m)L=\eta D_{\max}(R,C,n)+T_{\mathrm{prep}}(w_{\mathrm{cat}},m) and assume L≤TLML\leq T_{\mathrm{LM}}. Assume also that, under the ouroboros block layout introduced for the idle-frame-clearing schedule in Sec. XII.4.2, the transport routes serving simultaneous logical measurements do not cross one another. For a computation with at most kk simultaneous logical measurements, the handoff schedule can execute any sequence of measurement locations without transport delays using at most

Nbundle​(k,R,C,n,wcat,m)\displaystyle N_{\mathrm{bundle}}(k,R,C,n,w_{\mathrm{cat}},m) (8)
=k⁡(1+⌈2​[η​Dmax​(R,C,n)+Tprep​(wcat,m)]TLM⌉).\displaystyle=k\left(1+\left\lceil\frac{2\left[\eta D_{\max}(R,C,n)+T_{\mathrm{prep}}(w_{\mathrm{cat}},m)\right]}{T_{\mathrm{LM}}}\right\rceil\right).

In particular, two bundles per measurement stream suffice whenever

2​[η​Dmax​(R,C,n)+Tprep​(wcat,m)]≤TLM.2\left[\eta D_{\max}(R,C,n)+T_{\mathrm{prep}}(w_{\mathrm{cat}},m)\right]\leq T_{\mathrm{LM}}. (9)
Proof.

Partition the bundles among kk independent measurement streams. In each stream, use one trailing bundle and p=⌈2​L/TLM⌉p=\lceil 2L/T_{\mathrm{LM}}\rceil lookahead bundles. At the start of a logical measurement, the next lookahead bundle is already prepared at the target block and begins the measurement. The trailing bundle, released when the preceding logical measurement ended, travels to this same target and is prepared and verified in at most LL POCs. Because L≤TLML\leq T_{\mathrm{LM}}, it can take over before the current measurement ends.

This handoff releases the active lookahead bundle at most LL POCs after the measurement began. That bundle is next required pp measurements later, so it has at least p​TLM−L≥LpT_{\mathrm{LM}}-L\geq L POCs to travel to and prepare at its next assigned target. It is therefore ready before that measurement begins. Repeating the handoff gives a delay-free pipeline with p+1p+1 bundles per lane, which yields eq. 8. When 2​L≤TLM2L\leq T_{\mathrm{LM}}, p=1p=1: the leading bundle starts each target, the trailing bundle takes over, and the released leading bundle advances again. ∎

The 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1} device packs its 69 Q102 memory blocks and four Q102 Logical CliNR blocks in a nine-by-nine grid, as shown in Fig. 5. Consequently,

Dmax​(9,9,102)=102​(9−1)+5​(9−1)=856D_{\max}(9,9,102)=102(9-1)+5(9-1)=856 (10)

transport steps, or η​Dmax=42.8\eta D_{\max}=42.8 POCs for η=1/20\eta=1/20. The subsequent local preparation and verification takes Tprep​(30,2)=14.8T_{\mathrm{prep}}(30,2)=14.8 POCs, for a total lookahead time of 57.657.6 POCs. The two successive pipeline legs—bringing the trailing bundle to the active block and then sending the released lookahead bundle onward—take at most 2​(57.6)=115.22(57.6)=115.2 POCs. At the physical error rate p=10−4p=10^{-4}, a Viterbi measurement with cat-state weight wcat≥16w_{\mathrm{cat}}\geq 16 targeting a logical-measurement error rate of ϵ=10−10\epsilon=10^{-10} requires at least five SECs [78], hence TLM≥5​TSEC=135T_{\mathrm{LM}}\geq 5T_{\mathrm{SEC}}=135 POCs for Q102. Therefore

Nbundle​(k,9,9,102,30,2)\displaystyle N_{\mathrm{bundle}}(k,9,9,102,30,2) =k⁡(1+⌈2​(42.8+14.8)135⌉)\displaystyle=k\left(1+\left\lceil\frac{2(42.8+14.8)}{135}\right\rceil\right) (11)
=2​k.\displaystyle=2k.

Thus, two bundles suffice for each Q102 measurement stream. We call this stream-level allocation a cat-state bundle pair. One set of kk bundles can start the measurements at the current target blocks while the other set arrives, is prepared and verified, and takes over; the released set then moves ahead to the next kk targets. For the k=3k=3 measurements used by depth-one CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection, this requires three mobile cat-state bundle pairs (six individual bundles) rather than the 73​k=21973k=219 block-local bundles of the default Walking Cat architecture, a factor-36.5 reduction in spatial overhead without increasing logical-measurement latency.

The lookahead-based pipelining policy described above assumes that the target block of each lane is known at least LL POCs before its measurement begins. Feed-forward can violate this assumption when a measurement outcome determines which previously inactive code block is measured next: the released lookahead bundle has no unique destination until that outcome is available. A measurement on the selected block can then incur a stall of up to η​Dmax+Tprep​(wcat,m)=L\eta D_{\max}+T_{\mathrm{prep}}(w_{\mathrm{cat}},m)=L POCs while the leading bundle is transported, prepared, and verified. So, the delay-free guarantee of proposition 3 does not extend across such a conditional change of target block without provisioning bundles for the alternative destinations.

In the Walking Cat architecture, frame tracking does not cross code-block boundaries. Consequently, a tracked conditional Clifford gate may change a subsequent logical measurement by conjugating its observable, but it cannot change its target block. And, otherwise, we observe that no conditional operations in the actual compiled elliptic curve point addition circuits select among alternative destination blocks.

Let wmaxw_{\max} be the largest weight among the possible physical representatives of the conjugated logical observable. A weight-wmaxw_{\max} cat state can therefore be prepared at the known target before the frame is resolved. If the selected representative has lower weight, we pad it with identity factors to weight wmaxw_{\max}. The destination and cat-state size are therefore independent of the conditional outcome, so the handoff schedule remains applicable, with its preparation-time and bundle-count bounds evaluated at wcat=wmaxw_{\mathrm{cat}}=w_{\max}.

Under these constraints, kk cat-state bundle pairs, comprising 2​k2k individual bundles, suffice to pipeline the kk parallel logical measurements of depth-one CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection.

XII.4 The CLAW ISA and Depth-One CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} Injection

The Clifford-frame and Logical-operator Acceleration for Workloads (CLAW) ISA extends the logical instruction set of the Walking Cat architecture [78] with operations tailored to elliptic curve point addition circuits. It targets two principal bottlenecks in the compiled circuits. The first is the cost of implementing Clifford gates. Under the default Walking Cat assumptions, only pure-XX and pure-ZZ logical measurements are guaranteed to admit physical representatives of weight at most 30 and hence to be accessible using a weight-30 cat state. Tracking a Clifford gate such as a conditional CZ\mathrm{CZ} can conjugate these into more general Pauli measurements, so the baseline architecture cannot guarantee that every Clifford correction can be implemented by frame tracking. CLAW instead checks accessibility for the specific logical measurements required in the compiled elliptic curve point addition circuits. We compile each component assuming a clean input frame and use Monte Carlo sampling to check the conjugated logical measurements along its conditional Clifford trajectories. Every measurement encountered has an accessible Q102 physical representative of weight at most 30. Idle frame clearing, described in Sec. XII.4.2, maintains the clean-input-frame invariant without introducing additional runtime latency. This extension dramatically reduces the number of logical measurements required to implement Clifford gates in the elliptic-curve point-addition circuit, leaving Toffoli gates as the dominant runtime bottleneck.

To address this remaining bottleneck, we extend the CLAW ISA to include an LMP operation that measures in parallel any set of logical operators admitting pairwise-disjoint physical representatives; the corresponding measurement protocol is described in Sec. XII.4.1. In particular, the LMP operation allows the three disjoint logical measurements required for CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} state injection to be performed simultaneously, yielding an optimal depth-one implementation of the Toffoli gate as described in Sec. XII.4.3.

XII.4.1 Parallel Cat-State Measurements

We extend the cat-state measurement protocol of the Walking Cat architecture [78] to measure several logical Pauli operators in parallel. Let P1,…,PkP_{1},\ldots,P_{k} be logical operators with physical representatives P~1,…,P~k\widetilde{P}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{P}_{k} whose supports are pairwise disjoint. We insist upon disjointness here to enable a simple analysis of logical measurement fault rate–representatives with overlap may introduce correlated error when measured together. Additionally, for simplicity, suppose without loss of generality that every representative has weight wcatw_{\mathrm{cat}}. We prepare and verify kk distinct weight-wcatw_{\mathrm{cat}} cat states, one for each representative. The aath qubit of cat state CjC_{j} is coupled to the aath data qubit in the support of P~j\widetilde{P}_{j}. Because the data supports are disjoint, all k​wcatkw_{\mathrm{cat}} data–cat interactions can be scheduled in the same physical gate layer.

The kk verified cat states are placed side by side and transported as a single bundle. The bundle is slid into alignment with the union of the kk supports, the data–cat gates are applied simultaneously, and all cat qubits are then measured in the XX basis in the same readout round. Taking the parity of the outcomes within CjC_{j} yields the measurement bit for PjP_{j}, as illustrated for two parallel logical measurements in Fig. 10. This protocol then allows us to make kk logical measurements in a single physical measurement layer.

Because the physical representatives have disjoint supports, the corresponding measurements commute. Therefore, in the noiseless setting, executing the cat-state measurements in parallel is equivalent to executing them sequentially in any order. This guarantee persists under the swap-loss model because its faults are local. Each logical measurement uses a distinct cat state and a disjoint set of data–cat interactions, and faults are sampled locally for each physical operation. Consequently, no fault arising within one cat-state measurement—including a hook error or a swap induced by a lost ion—can propagate into another gadget. Parallel execution therefore leaves the outcome distribution and error probability of each logical measurement unchanged relative to executing that gadget alone in the same physical layer.

XII.4.2 Idle Frame Clearing

As in the Walking Cat architecture [78], we implement conditional Clifford corrections whenever possible by Clifford frame-tracking rather than applying them physically. The compiler updates the block’s Clifford frame UU and replaces each subsequent target logical Pauli operator PP by U†​P​UU^{\dagger}PU. When a subsequent non-Clifford operation requires a trivial Clifford frame, the tracked Clifford gate can be implemented using logical CliNR [81], thereby teleporting the encoded state into a block whose Clifford frame is reset to U=IU=I, as summarized in Fig. 11. We refer to this reset as clearing the Clifford frame. Because logical CliNR can be applied only once a block’s Clifford frame is known, frame clearing is generally bottlenecked by resolving the classical conditions associated with conditional Clifford gates. That generally means it’s only safe to apply logical CliNR once the block becomes idle, or we must actively pause execution to clear the frame. Logical CliNR uses two auxiliary memory blocks, AA and BB, as resource blocks; both are encoded using the same code as the data block whose frame is being cleared. At completion, the logical state of the cleaned block has been teleported to BB, whose Clifford frame is trivial, while the original data block and AA can be reset and reused.

Optimizing the CLAW ISA for elliptic curve point addition circuits requires identifying the precise set of logical Pauli operators actually measured by each compiled component. To make this tractable, we compile components independently under an invariant: each memory block in a component’s support has a trivial Clifford frame immediately before its first non-Clifford use. To enforce this invariant, we must use frame clearing on each block in a component’s support.

Frame clearing can run in parallel with logical measurements on other blocks. Because most components of the elliptic-curve point-addition circuit are serial, each block is idle long enough to clear its frame without extending the critical path. More generally, the elliptic-curve circuits consist of a sequence of components that act serially on ordered sets of logical blocks: each component proceeds down its blocks and then uncomputes in reverse order, with occasional shallow layers of parallel gates between components; see Fig. 12. We call these components serial components.

We therefore pipeline frame clearing ahead of each serial component’s execution, as illustrated in Fig. 13.

However, in order to keep up with the serial execution, we must ensure that logical CliNR can clear a block in less time than the serial execution takes to process all measurements in a code block. To achieve this, we optimize logical CliNR by measuring MECM stages in parallel when they are compatible under the rules of parallel cat-state measurements. Within each MECM stage, we connect two outputs in a compatibility graph when their physical representatives can be chosen with disjoint supports on both CliNR resource blocks and with weight at most 30, then find a maximum matching; unmatched stages are measured individually. By sampling uniformly from the Clifford frames encountered in a simulation of the compiled elliptic-curve point-addition circuit, we find that the optimized MECM portion of a frame clear takes 41.242±0.27641.242\pm 0.276 Q102 SEC layers. The transversal CNOT\mathrm{CNOT} gate is followed by one additional Q102 SEC for decoding, so a complete frame clear takes 42.242±0.27642.242\pm 0.276 Q102 SECs. Using the joint CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection duration of approximately 5.465.46 Q102 SECs derived in eq. 26, this corresponds to approximately 7.737.73 logical-measurement intervals to clear a block. The serial components expose a new block after approximately 7.57.5 such intervals; it therefore requires at least two instances of logical CliNR to keep up with the serial execution.

Because we apply logical CliNR only to serial components, the compiler can lay out the data blocks used by those components as an ordered register following their serial traversal order. The timing estimate above shows that two logical CliNR instances are required to ensure that frames are always cleared ahead of serial execution. We divide the register between them by alternating blocks: one instance clears the blocks in even positions, and the other clears those in odd positions. Thus, each instance clears only every other block. Since, typically, execution of serial components in the elliptic curve point addition circuits reaches a new block every 7.57.5 logical-measurement intervals, each CliNR instance has 2×7.5=152\times 7.5=15 intervals before it is needed again, enough time to clear a block in approximately 7.737.73 intervals.

The transversal CNOT\mathrm{CNOT} gate in logical CliNR requires data qubits to be transported close to each other to perform pairwise physical CNOT\mathrm{CNOT} gates. We therefore keep the AA resource block in the logical CliNR protocol adjacent to the data block during injection. Each data qubit then moves by at most the width of one Q102 block to interact with its corresponding resource qubit, minimizing errors due to idling, loss, and leakage during transport.

The 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1} device introduced in Sec. XII.1 has a 69-data-block register. Assigning alternating blocks to the two logical CliNR instances divides this register into groups of 35 and 34 data blocks. Adding one A/BA/B resource pair, or two blocks, to each group gives 37 and 36 blocks. Each group fits on a closed nearest-neighbor path through a 4×104\times 10 rectangle, which provides 40 cells. The two rectangles therefore leave three and four cells empty, respectively. Stacking them gives an 8×108\times 10 layout containing the 69 data blocks, four resource blocks, and seven empty cells. We call this assignment of the alternating block subsequences and their resource pairs to closed nearest-neighbor paths the ouroboros block layout. As the application processes further serial components, the compiler can append each new traversal to the end of the current execution path, which wraps in a circular pattern around the data blocks—hence the name “ouroboros.”

Under the ouroboros block layout, it remains to show that each logical CliNR instance can follow the path of serial execution on its data blocks while retaining nearest-neighbor locality with the next target (and, with this condition, execute a transversal CNOT\mathrm{CNOT} gate with minimal overhead). A single application of logical CliNR results in a swap of the BB and data blocks, leaving AA adjacent to the next data block. If DiD_{i} has no frame to clear, one can simply cyclically shift the blocks, implemented by swapping corresponding physical qubits between the blocks. Induction over these local permutations shows that the resource pair remains adjacent to its next target for the entire sequence of clearing a serial application component ahead of execution. Fig. 14 illustrates the ouroboros block layout for cleaning three partially overlapping serial components.

The ouroboros block layout also accommodates a component that starts within the support of its predecessor. In this case, the logical CliNR instance follows the predecessor’s execution across the “ascending” execution of logical measurements, cleaning the frame of blocks with a nontrivial frame and simply making full-block swaps to the intervening blocks whose frames are already clean. They may stop as soon as they reach the first target of the later component; see Fig. 15. In the worst case, the last block released by the earlier component is also the first block required by the later one. Its clearing cannot be hidden behind earlier execution, so the transition stalls for one logical CliNR operation, or approximately 7.737.73 logical-measurement intervals.

XII.4.3 Depth-One CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} Injection

As shown in Fig. 16, a Toffoli gate is a CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} gate conjugated by Hadamard gates on its target qubit. The CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} gate can be injected via one-bit gate teleportation [73, 86] by measuring a joint logical- ZZ operator between each qubit of the CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} resource state and the corresponding data qubit, followed by destructive XX-basis measurements of the resource qubits and outcome-dependent corrections. The three joint logical- ZZ measurements have disjoint supports and can therefore be performed in parallel, so the injection requires only one logical-measurement layer. The subsequent XX-basis outcomes induce only Pauli corrections, which can be tracked in a Pauli frame and need not be available until the following gate has completed. Their readout is generally faster than the 5.465.46 Q102 SECs required for the joint logical measurements, and hence does not add another layer to the critical path. Lastly, the compiler ensures that both operands of every conditional CZ\mathrm{CZ} correction reside in the same memory block, as described in Sec. X, so each correction can be absorbed into the block’s Clifford frame without adding a logical-measurement layer.

We quantify the measurement depth after compilation using Monte Carlo simulation. For each independently compiled circuit component, we draw 10,00010{,}000 samples of random outcomes for conditional Clifford corrections. Each sample begins with a trivial Clifford frame on every input block, as required by the compilation invariant and guaranteed during execution by the idle-frame-clearing procedure of Sec. XII.4.2. After propagating the sampled Clifford frames and scheduling the resulting logical measurements, we find that every sampled conjugated logical operator has an accessible physical representative. The empirical frequency resolution is therefore 10−410^{-4} per component; under independent sampling, observing no inaccessible trajectory gives the one-sided 95%95\% upper confidence bound 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} on the probability that a trajectory contains an inaccessible logical operator, for each component. Through this simulation of all the application components, we find that 93.6%93.6\% of Toffoli gates have measurement depth one. The remaining gates require depth two, giving a mean measurement depth of 1.071.07.

XII.5 Eastinthillation CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} Factory

We design a dedicated “Eastinthillation” factory (Eastin + synthillation) that produces CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} states directly in a three-ring code block. We note that the alternative name “East Mode” may be used in less formal contexts— for instance, in fan-made songs about this paper. The Eastinthillation factory’s resource totals and performance estimates are summarized below.

The factory applies the Eastin Toffoli-state synthillation protocol [24, 12] to eight TT states produced by zero-level distillation in the [[6,2,2]][\![6,2,2]\!] code (henceforth referred to as the C6 code). This TT-state distillation procedure is detailed in Sec. XII.5.1. On acceptance, the protocol outputs a Toffoli state. Applying a Hadamard to its target qubit converts it into a CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} resource state. The Eastinthillation factory circuit and its physical measurement schedule are described in Sec. XII.5.2, while Sec. XII.5.3 analyzes the factory’s logical error and rejection rates, depth, and physical-qubit footprint. Finally we describe how to adapt the Eastinthillation factory to produce the TT states required for the QFT stage of Shor’s algorithm in Sec. XII.5.4.

XII.5.1 0-Level TT-State Distillation

We prepare each pair of |H⟩\ket{H} states using the protocol of Dasu et al. [21]. The protocol uses Goto’s arbitrary-state encoder [32] to encode the states in the C6 code before joint logical-Hadamard verification and syndrome extraction. The two verified |H⟩\ket{H} states remain encoded and are consumed through the dual-TT-state injection circuit of the Walking Cat architecture [78]. The joint verification measures HL,0​HL,1H_{\mathrm{L},0}H_{\mathrm{L},1} using a two-qubit Bell state. A flagged readout followed by C6 syndrome extraction makes this measurement fault-tolerant.

The preparation circuit for two logical |H⟩\ket{H} states in the C6 code is shown in Fig. 17. As a three-ring code, we may implement the C6 code’s SEC circuit with cyclic shifts, but the encoding circuit’s connectivity cannot be achieved with just cyclic shifts. We instead propose using a short sequence of column swaps to implement the encoding circuit. Separate loss and leakage checks are unnecessary for this error-detecting code block because every qubit is destructively measured with loss-and-leakage detection during either state preparation or consumption.

We simulated the state-preparation, verification, and SEC circuit using the statevector method in Qiskit Aer. The logical error and rejection rates in Table 8 are Monte Carlo estimates with 10910^{9} shots using the swap loss noise model at p=10−4p=10^{-4}. The simulator appends ideal, destructive measurements of the two logical Hadamard operators HL,0H_{\mathrm{L},0} and HL,1H_{\mathrm{L},1} to estimate logical fidelity. The results of this simulation are included in Table 8, which also reports the depth and physical-qubit footprint of the circuit.

XII.5.2 Eastinthillation factory circuit

The Eastinthillation factory circuit, based on the Eastin Toffoli-state synthillation protocol [24], is shown in Fig. 18. The protocol uses eight |H⟩\ket{H} states from the zero-level factories based on the C6 code to implement two Margolus–Toffoli gates with shared controls and distinct targets. Let pY,injp_{Y,\mathrm{inj}} denote the stochastic logical-YY fault probability per |H⟩\ket{H}-state injection used to implement a logical RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) rotation. A final “acceptance” parity check on the targets detects any single stochastic-YY input fault and yields a Toffoli state with error probability of order pY,inj2p_{Y,\mathrm{inj}}^{2}. We apply a Hadamard to the target qubit of the accepted Toffoli state. This final Clifford converts it into a CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} resource state compatible with the depth-one CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} gate of Sec. XII.4.

We implement the Eastinthillation factory circuit in a single Q66 code block using the measurement-layer sequence shown in Fig. 19. The measurements use the LM1, LM2, and DM operations from the Walking Cat instruction set [78], mediated by EDM (error-detecting measurement) and Viterbi measurement schemes. We extend these schemes to include the Multi-Pauli error-corrected measurement operation (MECM) introduced by Webster and Delfosse [81].

Every cat-state-mediated measurement layer in Fig. 19 admits physical representatives whose supports on the GB66 block are pairwise disjoint, with each representative having weight at most 16. The complete representative certificates are given in appendix G. The relatively small width of these representatives allows us to use only 3 rounds of EDM for each double-RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection to achieve a pHp_{H} of order 10−810^{-8} at physical error rate p=10−4p=10^{-4}. Similarly, we require only 5 rounds of Viterbi measurements to achieve logical error rates of order 10−1310^{-13}. Each double-RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection ends in a DMX – a destructive readout of all data qubits in the H6 block, an operation which takes only 1 POC to execute regardless of width.

RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection.

Each pair of RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) rotations is implemented with the double-RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection gadget of the Walking Cat architecture [78], which involves a joint Y​YYY measurement followed by a DMX operation on the C6 block. To avoid correlated input errors, each Q66 block has two dedicated C6 source blocks. A double-RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) layer takes one logical qubit, prepared in |H⟩\ket{H}, from each C6 block rather than taking both inputs from one encoded |H⟩⊗2\ket{H}^{\otimes 2} pair. The terminal DMX consumes both C6 blocks, including the unused logical qubit in each block. The two blocks are then reinitialized and their next encoded |H⟩⊗2\ket{H}^{\otimes 2} pairs are prepared and verified in parallel for the same Q66 block. We use dedicated C6 blocks rather than sharing them among multiple Q66 blocks. This choice simplifies the factory analysis by eliminating contention for shared resources.

Within either source C6 block, the two logical-YY operators have representatives

Y¯0=YIYIYI,Y¯1=IYIYIY.\overline{Y}_{0}=\texttt{YIYIYI},\qquad\overline{Y}_{1}=\texttt{IYIYIY}. (12)

These representatives have disjoint supports and weight three. Nevertheless, either operator can be measured using a two-qubit cat-state segment (a Bell state) by reusing one cat qubit for two data interactions. This reuse does not reduce the measurement distance. A fault on the reused cat qubit can propagate to two C6 data qubits. We choose the data-qubit support of each cat-state qubit so that no resulting hook error is a nontrivial C6 logical operator. Every such error has a nonzero syndrome and is rejected by the following SEC.

Combining the two-qubit C6 segment with a Q66 representative of weight at most 16 gives a weight-18 cat state for the joint YC6​YQ66Y_{\mathrm{C6}}Y_{\mathrm{Q66}} observable in the double-RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection.

Each Q66 cat-state factory contains two cat-state registers and one verification bank, all provisioned at width 16. Increasing one factory’s width to 18 therefore requires 3​(18−16)=63(18-16)=6 additional qubits. We keep a six-qubit C6 Bell-state source next to each C6 block. For C6 state verification, two of these qubits form the Bell state described above. During the joint YC6​YQ66Y_{\mathrm{C6}}Y_{\mathrm{Q66}} measurement, however, all six qubits are loaned to the weight 16 Q66 cat-state factory so it may create a weight 18 cat state. These two operations do not overlap, so the same C6 Bell-state source can support both.

The logical measurement still contains 19 data–cat interactions, so the logical-measurement error estimate below uses effective width weff=19w_{\mathrm{eff}}=19.

At weff=19w_{\mathrm{eff}}=19 and p=10−4p=10^{-4}, the fitted EDM model of Ref. [78] gives the single-round outcome-flip probability

pflip≃2.1​weff​p=3.99×10−3.p_{\mathrm{flip}}\simeq 2.1w_{\mathrm{eff}}p=3.99\times 10^{-3}. (13)

It takes three EDM rounds to suppress the measurement-induced error to the same order of magnitude as the state preparation error (pH2p_{H^{2}}), since pflip2=1.59×10−5p_{\mathrm{flip}}^{2}=1.59\times 10^{-5} whereas pflip3=6.35×10−8p_{\mathrm{flip}}^{3}=6.35\times 10^{-8}. We therefore use EDM-3 for each RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection. Its logical-outcome error rate is

pEDM3≃pflip3=6.35×10−8.p_{\mathrm{EDM3}}\simeq p_{\mathrm{flip}}^{3}=6.35\times 10^{-8}. (14)

An EDM-3 outcome sequence is accepted when its three outcomes are all correct or all flipped. The two inputs to a double injection come from the two dedicated C6 blocks of the same Eastinthillation factory. Each input undergoes three C6 SECs, and the factory accepts only if both C6 blocks accept all three. Using the common C6 SEC rejection rate rSECC6=0.323%r_{\mathrm{SEC}}^{\mathrm{C6}}=0.323\%, the per-injection acceptance factor is therefore

aRY=[(1−pflip)3+pflip3]​(1−rSECC6)3=0.978534.a_{R_{Y}}=\bigl[(1-p_{\mathrm{flip}})^{3}+p_{\mathrm{flip}}^{3}\bigr](1-r_{\mathrm{SEC}}^{\mathrm{C6}})^{3}=0.978534. (15)

The corresponding rejection rate is rRY=1−aRY=2.147%r_{R_{Y}}=1-a_{R_{Y}}=2.147\%. The factor aRY8a_{R_{Y}}^{8} accounts for the eight EDM-3 outcome sequences and the 24 C6 SECs required by one CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} preparation attempt.

The parity check at the end of the Eastinthillation factory can only detect single-logical-qubit YY or XX errors; and all errors in the synthillation protocol can effectively be traced to RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injections. So we would like to ensure that RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection errors are only either YY- or XX-type errors. We rely on the injected-YY noise model of the Walking Cat architecture [78]: conditioned on the EDM and SEC acceptance tests, an injection fault is represented by a stochastic logical YY on the corresponding Q66 qubit. This follows from analyzing the conditional corrections of the logical measurements involved in the RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injection. A wrong terminal DMX result erroneously applies a YY correction. A wrong EDM result applies a ZC6​RY​(π/2)Q66Z_{\mathrm{C6}}R_{Y}(\pi/2)_{\mathrm{Q66}} error; the extra ZC6Z_{\mathrm{C6}} triggers the subsequent C6 XX readout and therefore also applies a YY error via DMX YY correction (so, at the very least, is always correlated with a YY error). The residual Q66 operation is RY(π/2)Y≐RY(−π/2)R_{Y}(\pi/2)Y\doteq R_{Y}(-\pi/2), or the inverse rotation. The source |H⟩\ket{H} state has zero YY expectation. The two outcomes of the joint YC6​YQ66Y_{\mathrm{C6}}Y_{\mathrm{Q66}} measurement, and hence the two residual rotations, are equiprobable. Averaging the corresponding channels gives

12ℛY,π/2+12ℛY,−π/2=12ℐ+12𝒴,\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{Y,\pi/2}+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{Y,-\pi/2}=\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{Y}, (16)

where ℛY,θ\mathcal{R}_{Y,\theta} is the channel induced by RY​(θ)R_{Y}(\theta) and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is conjugation by logical YY. We therefore bound the stochastic logical-YY fault rate by the full EDM-3 logical-outcome error probability.

The two input states in each injection layer have independent preparation errors because they come from distinct C6 blocks. Because faults at these locations are sampled independently, the preparation errors are also independent. Consequently, for a single injection, the marginal stochastic logical-YY probability is bounded by the sum of the preparation and EDM-3 error probabilities:

pY,inj≲pH2+pEDM3=7.65×10−8.p_{Y,\mathrm{inj}}\lesssim p_{H^{2}}+p_{\mathrm{EDM3}}=7.65\times 10^{-8}. (17)
Acceptance Measurement.

The acceptance measurement uses a LM1 operation mediated by Viterbi measurement. Its representative has weight 16, so wcat=16w_{\mathrm{cat}}=16, as shown in Table 16. At p=10−4p=10^{-4}, the single-round bit-flip model of Ref. [78] gives

pflip,16=2.1​wcat​p=2.1×16×10−4=3.36×10−3.p_{\mathrm{flip},16}=2.1w_{\mathrm{cat}}p=2.1\times 16\times 10^{-4}=3.36\times 10^{-3}. (18)

For target error ε=10−11\varepsilon=10^{-11}, the Viterbi stopping condition requires vote margin

d16=⌈log⁡[(1−ε)/ε]log⁡[(1−pflip,16)/pflip,16]⌉=5.d_{16}=\left\lceil\frac{\log[(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon]}{\log[(1-p_{\mathrm{flip},16})/p_{\mathrm{flip},16}]}\right\rceil=5. (19)

The logical error is therefore

pVit,16=[1+(1−pflip,16pflip,16)5]−1=4.36×10−13.p_{\mathrm{Vit},16}=\left[1+\left(\frac{1-p_{\mathrm{flip},16}}{p_{\mathrm{flip},16}}\right)^{5}\right]^{-1}=4.36\times 10^{-13}. (20)

The cat-state rejection model of Ref. [78] gives pmiss,16=5​wcat​p=8.0×10−3p_{\mathrm{miss},16}=5w_{\mathrm{cat}}p=8.0\times 10^{-3}. Writing ρ16=pflip,16/(1−pflip,16)\rho_{16}=p_{\mathrm{flip},16}/(1-p_{\mathrm{flip},16}), the average duration is

τVit,16avg=11−pmiss,16​d161−2​pflip,16​1−ρ16d161+ρ16d16=5.07​SEC.\tau_{\mathrm{Vit},16}^{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{1-p_{\mathrm{miss},16}}\frac{d_{16}}{1-2p_{\mathrm{flip},16}}\frac{1-\rho_{16}^{d_{16}}}{1+\rho_{16}^{d_{16}}}=5.07~\mathrm{SEC}. (21)
CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} Injection.

The three CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection measurements follow the protocol of Sec. XII.4. The largest joint representative has weight 36, with weight 20 from the Q102 logical ZZ operator and weight 16 from the Q66 logical ZZ operator. We therefore use wcat=36w_{\mathrm{cat}}=36 for all three measurements to deduce an upper bound on the logical error of the measurements. At p=10−4p=10^{-4}, the single-round bit-flip probability is

pflip,36=2.1×36×10−4=7.56×10−3.p_{\mathrm{flip},36}=2.1\times 36\times 10^{-4}=7.56\times 10^{-3}. (22)

For target error ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10}, the Viterbi stopping condition requires vote margin

d36=⌈log⁡[(1−ε)/ε]log⁡[(1−pflip,36)/pflip,36]⌉=5.d_{36}=\left\lceil\frac{\log[(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon]}{\log[(1-p_{\mathrm{flip},36})/p_{\mathrm{flip},36}]}\right\rceil=5. (23)

The logical error per measurement is therefore

pVit,36=[1+(1−pflip,36pflip,36)5]−1=2.57×10−11.p_{\mathrm{Vit},36}=\left[1+\left(\frac{1-p_{\mathrm{flip},36}}{p_{\mathrm{flip},36}}\right)^{5}\right]^{-1}=2.57\times 10^{-11}. (24)

The cat-state rejection model of Ref. [78] gives pmiss,36=5​wcat​p=1.8×10−2p_{\mathrm{miss},36}=5w_{\mathrm{cat}}p=1.8\times 10^{-2}. Writing ρ36=pflip,36/(1−pflip,36)\rho_{36}=p_{\mathrm{flip},36}/(1-p_{\mathrm{flip},36}), the average duration of one Viterbi measurement is

Phase Fixups.

After the three CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection measurements, we measure the three commuting resource-block observables P0,P1,P2P_{0},P_{1},P_{2} obtained by conjugating the logical-XX operators by the tracked Clifford frame. This frame includes one conditional Clifford correction from each of the eight RY​(π/4)R_{Y}(\pi/4) injections, so we analyze all 28=2562^{8}=256 frame branches.

We call a destructive readout that measures each physical data qubit in an independently chosen Pauli basis a generalized destructive measurement (DMG). A single DMG measures logical Pauli observables with pairwise-disjoint physical representatives in parallel: on the support of each representative, the physical qubits are measured in the corresponding single-qubit Pauli bases. A DMG takes only one POC–less than a full SEC.

Pairwise-disjoint representatives of all three PiP_{i} are not available on every branch. When they are available, a single DMG measures the three PiP_{i} in parallel. If exactly one pair overlaps, we measure one member of that pair using a single Viterbi measurement. We then measure the other two observables, whose representatives are disjoint, in parallel with a single DMG. If every pair overlaps, we measure products of the PiP_{i} that admit disjoint representatives. In both cases requiring nondestructive logical measurement layers, only one such layer precedes the terminal DMG. The phase fixups therefore require at most one measurement layer.

We describe the MECM and Viterbi cases using the scheduler-matrix convention of Ref. [81]: for G∈𝔽23×3G\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{3\times 3}, column jj specifies the observable

Qj=∏i=02PiGi​j.Q_{j}=\prod_{i=0}^{2}P_{i}^{G_{ij}}. (27)

If the eigenvalues of PiP_{i} and QjQ_{j} are (−1)ui(-1)^{u_{i}} and (−1)vj(-1)^{v_{j}}, respectively, then

v=u​G,u=v​G−1.v=uG,\qquad u=vG^{-1}. (28)

An invertible GG therefore replaces the PiP_{i} with an equivalent set of logical observables QjQ_{j}. Measuring the QjQ_{j} gives the same logical information because uu can be recovered from vv, and it requires no additional measurement layer.

Only two scheduler matrices are required:

Gid=(100010001),Gprod=(101010001).G_{\mathrm{id}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad G_{\mathrm{prod}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. (29)

GidG_{\mathrm{id}} measures Qi=PiQ_{i}=P_{i} – it is no different from an ordinary Viterbi measurement. On the 32 branches whose original generators ordinarily require three measurement layers, GprodG_{\mathrm{prod}} replaces P2P_{2} with the equivalent generator P0​P2P_{0}P_{2}, so that it measures

(Q0,Q1,Q2)=(P0,P1,P0​P2).(Q_{0},Q_{1},Q_{2})=(P_{0},P_{1},P_{0}P_{2}). (30)

Since Gprod−1=GprodG_{\mathrm{prod}}^{-1}=G_{\mathrm{prod}}, the original outcomes are

u0=v0,u1=v1,u2=v0+v2(mod2).u_{0}=v_{0},\qquad u_{1}=v_{1},\qquad u_{2}=v_{0}+v_{2}\pmod{2}. (31)

.

Table 9 gives the resulting schedule for all 256 frame branches. On 32 branches, the three QjQ_{j} share a physical product basis and are obtained in parallel with a single DMG. On each of the other 224 branches, one QjQ_{j} is measured by a Viterbi measurement before the remaining pair is obtained in parallel with a single DMG. On the branches using Q2=P0​P2Q_{2}=P_{0}P_{2}, Q1Q_{1} and Q2Q_{2} have compatible, disjoint physical representatives even though the three original generators cannot be partitioned into fewer than three compatible layers. All QjQ_{j} commute, so the Viterbi measurement layer can be measured before the DMG layer. Physical representatives for the MECM and DMG layers are given in Tables 18, 19 and 20.

As established in appendix G, the physical representative has weight at most 16, so its outcome-flip probability is pflip,16=3.36×10−3p_{\mathrm{flip},16}=3.36\times 10^{-3}. Factory footprint.

We say that a number of factories is sufficient to produce a continuous stream of CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} states if, collectively, their average time to produce a magic state is shorter than the average time per state injection. The point-addition circuit executes at most one Toffoli gate at a time. A Q102 memory block occupies the CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection interface for τCCZavg≈5.46\tau_{\mathrm{CCZ}}^{\mathrm{avg}}\approx 5.46 Q102 SECs and can therefore consume at most one CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} state every Tinj=147.48T_{\mathrm{inj}}=147.48 POCs. Since one factory supplies an accepted state every 555.75555.75 POCs on average, the number of factories required to maintain this consumption rate is

NCCZ=⌈T¯factoryτCCZavg​TSECQ102⌉=⌈555.75147.48⌉=4.N_{\mathrm{CCZ}}=\left\lceil\frac{\overline{T}_{\mathrm{factory}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{CCZ}}^{\mathrm{avg}}T_{\mathrm{SEC}}^{\mathrm{Q102}}}\right\rceil=\left\lceil\frac{555.75}{147.48}\right\rceil=4. (56)

Each Eastinthillation factory uses one Q66 block, three weight-16 cat-state factories, two dedicated zero-level C6 source blocks, and one six-qubit C6 Bell-state source per C6 block. As derived in Sec. E.1, this gives 319 physical qubits per factory and 1,276 physical qubits for all four factories. The resulting layout is shown in Fig. 20.

Q66 memory errors give the largest contribution to this bound by two orders of magnitude; the scheme is otherwise capable of producing CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} gates with logical error rate of order 1e-13. This floor can be met by higher-distance code or a decoder that uses loss and leakage information, e.g.  [54]. Or, one may exploit soft information in the decoder: the factory can reject and restart low-confidence attempts before their outputs are used [8, 75].

XII.5.4 T-state factory conversion

The windowed semiclassical iQFT requires arbitrary-angle ZZ-rotations, which can be synthesized approximately with TT gates using the mixing+fallback method [47]. We only need 16 ZZ-rotations per window if we execute them sequentially, feedforward measurement results and calculate the angles from the accumulated measurement outcomes. The total number of ZZ-rotations across all iQFTs is 464, with 0.57​log2⁡(1/ε)+8.830.57\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon)+8.83 TT gates per rotation, where ε\varepsilon is the approximation error per rotation.

However, the Eastinthillation factory can prepare only CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} states. We can repurpose its components to produce TT states instead. The local C6 TT-state factories inject the required TT states into the Q66 blocks, where they can be safely stored in memory. The states are then teleported to the Q102 blocks as required. Using the measured logical error rate of 1.30×10−81.30\times 10^{-8} per accepted pair, and minimizing for the total diamond-norm distance, we obtain the optimal ε=5.30×10−9\varepsilon=5.30\times 10^{-9} and the average TT-sequence length 24.5. This results in an expected total of 5,684 required TT pairs.

This gives the total iQFT-stage failure probability, by the union bound, at most

piQFT≤5,684​(1.30×10−8)+464​(5.30×10−9)=\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{iQFT}}\leq 5{,}684\left(1.30\times 10^{-8}\right)+464\left(5.30\times 10^{-9}\right)=
=7.64×10−5.\displaystyle=7.64\times 10^{-5}. (61)

Part VI Conclusion

We presented optimized quantum circuits for solving the ECDLP on 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1} using Shor’s algorithm, derived rigorous bounds on the success probability of the implementation—taking into account phase- and output-errors due to approximate arithmetic—and compiled our implementation to our application-specific extension of the Walking Cat architecture [78] using our compilation toolchain, allowing us to accurately account for the overheads due to layout and routing. By combining quantum-circuit, compilation, and architecture improvements, we showed that a trapped-ion quantum computer with 20,00020{,}000 qubits should be able to solve the ECDLP on 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1} within 26 days. Because we intentionally prioritize simple, uniform implementations over exhaustive co-optimization, we expect future work to improve the runtime, physical-qubit footprint, and success probability reported here.

In our resource estimates, we have taken into account hardware details that have typically been ignored in the literature. This enables us to be more confident about our runtime and footprint estimates. For instance, one of the major issues with trapped-ion architectures (and one we prominently addressed in the original Walking Cat architecture) is a loss cascade. When an ion is lost, if its well is merged with that of a second ion to perform a two-qubit gate, the electrode configuration will not be correct for optimal trapping. This can result in substantial heating of the remaining ion, which can lead to ejection from the trap. The leakage and loss reduction units (LLRUs) developed in that architecture assume that this ejection happens 100%100\% of the time. However, for sufficiently deep traps, this might not be the case. Here, we use a different loss propagation model in which the ion is not ejected but its final position after a split is randomized, and we develop a new LLRU to address this model of loss propagation. We expect that the physical situation is more nuanced, with heating and ejection considered using a detailed microarchitecture, but we leave this to future work.

Several of our techniques could also reduce the resource requirements of other fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, e.g., for chemistry, condensed matter physics, and optimization [2, 20]. In particular, the Clifford frame clearing using logical CliNR and our integrated routing can be included in the general-purpose Walking Cat architecture without any additional hardware requirements. The increased logical-measurement parallelism obtained using non-overlapping cat-based measurements is straightforward to include in the Walking Cat architecture at the price of adjusting the block allocation to allow for increased cat state throughput in the vicinity of the target blocks. Lastly, our fast CCZ implementation provides a 31×31\times speedup over a CCZ compiled into Clifford and TT gates. We leave it to future work to quantify the impact of these optimizations on quantum computing applications beyond the ECDLP.

Part VII Appendix

Appendix A Algorithms

A.1 Affine elliptic curve point addition

This section contains integer-valued representations of the algorithms that comprise the affine elliptic curve point addition circuits in our implementation. Algorithm 3 shows the classical precomputation of the initial accumulator point and the lookup tables for each window in the point addition loop shown in Algorithm 4. There are L=⌈n/w⌉L=\lceil n/w\rceil windows of size ww with the top window possibly containing less than ww bits. After sampling the random initialization point [a]​P[a]P by sampling a uniform random a∈ℤr∗a\in\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{*}, Algorithm 3 first computes the LL tables with multiples of the base point PP, then the LL tables with multiples of the point QQ of which we seek to compute the discrete logarithm with respect to base PP. It also computes and stores 3⋅x3\cdot x for the xx-coordinates of all points in the table.

Algorithm 4 is a simple loop over all 2​L2L windows that just adds the respective table points. Note that the scalars kk and ll are decomposed into their windowed 2w2^{w}-ary representations

k=∑i=0L−1ki​2i​w,l=∑i=0L−1li​2i​w,k=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}k_{i}2^{iw},\quad l=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}l_{i}2^{iw},

and the digits kik_{i} and lil_{i} are used to look up the correct table points that are passed to the affine addition AffineAdd\mathrm{AffineAdd} depicted in Algorithm 5. In practice, we use w=16w=16 and we only perform 2828 of the 3232 point additions as described in [51]: We replace the first point addition by a table lookup and drop the final 33 windowed point additions in favor of extended classical postprocessing [26]. We start with the ww most-significant bits of the first scalar and move toward the least-significant bit in each step, implementing the semi-classical quantum Fourier transform in blocks of size ww [34].

The affine addition algorithm 𝖠𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖾𝖠𝖽𝖽\mathsf{AffineAdd} uses the following subroutines. 𝖡𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗋𝗒𝖦𝖢𝖣𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽\mathsf{BinaryGCDRecord} consumes its input and retains the compressed Dialog/add-sub record. 𝖡𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗋𝗒𝖦𝖢𝖣𝖨𝗇𝗏𝖬𝗎𝗅\mathsf{BinaryGCDInvMul} and 𝖡𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗋𝗒𝖦𝖢𝖣𝖬𝗎𝗅\mathsf{BinaryGCDMul} replay it to compute the in-place division or in-place multiplication, respectively, and 𝖡𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗋𝗒𝖦𝖢𝖣𝖴𝗇𝗋𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖽\mathsf{BinaryGCDUnrecord} restores the input and clears all record scratch. The two replays use modular halvings and doublings, respectively.

The notation 𝖫𝗈𝗈𝗄𝗎𝗉(x,y)\mathsf{Lookup}_{(x,y)} or 𝖫𝗈𝗈𝗄𝗎𝗉3​x\mathsf{Lookup}_{3x} loads the indicated coordinates, while m←𝖷𝖢𝗅𝖾𝖺𝗋⁡(u)m\leftarrow\mathsf{XClear}(u) measures and clears a lookup register and records its XX-basis outcome. The square-subtract circuit is the one-split Karatsuba version specific for 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1}. Note that we classically sample a uniform random mask R∈𝔽pR\in\mathbb{F}_{p} and add it with an approximate quantum-classical adder to the xx-register before the lookup of the xx-coordinate multiple. This randomizes the accumulator register in the square-sub circuit. The mask is removed after the subtraction of the square by an approximate addition of −Rmodp-R\bmod p. The separate addition step x←(x+R)modpx\leftarrow(x+R)\bmod p can be omitted if a fresh offset RiR_{i} is sampled for the ii-th window in Algorithm 3 during the generation of the lookup tables. The table would then contain 3​xi,j+Ri3x_{i,j}+R_{i} instead of 3​xi,j3x_{i,j} and the masked value would be looked up, making the separate addition unnecessary.

Appendix B Failure case analysis

As in essentially all previous work (see, e.g., [64, 35, 69, 33, 51, 3, 71]), the elliptic curve point addition circuits described here are approximate, which means there exist inputs for which the circuits fail to compute the correct result for reasons from two different categories. Failures in the first category occur when the input elliptic curve points constitute an exceptional case where the underlying addition formula fails. Failures in the second category are due to an approximate modular arithmetic component failing to produce the exact intended result. This section shows that the overall number of failure cases occurring in our proposed randomized circuit for affine point addition is small enough to allow the full Shor algorithm to succeed with high probability. In particular, we show that for each pair of scalars (k,l)(k,l), the probability that it leads to a failure case is bounded by a constant pfp_{f} independent of kk and ll.

B.1 Exceptional cases for elliptic curve point addition

As in most previous work, we use the affine point addition formula for the short Weierstrass model E:y2=x3+a​x+bE:y^{2}=x^{3}+ax+b. Given P1=(x1,y1)P_{1}=(x_{1},y_{1}) and P2=(x2,y2)P_{2}=(x_{2},y_{2}), the point P3=(x3,y3)=P1+P2P_{3}=(x_{3},y_{3})=P_{1}+P_{2} is computed as x3=λ2−x1−x2x_{3}=\lambda^{2}-x_{1}-x_{2} and y3=(x2−x3)​λ−y2y_{3}=(x_{2}-x_{3})\lambda-y_{2}, where λ=(y2−y1)/(x2−x1)\lambda=(y_{2}-y_{1})/(x_{2}-x_{1}). This formula has exceptional cases. It cannot be used if x2=x1x_{2}=x_{1}, i.e., if P1=±P2P_{1}=\pm P_{2}, and also if one of the points is the point at infinity 𝒪\mathcal{O}. Because quantum circuits can only implement reversible operations, the slope value λ\lambda is often uncomputed from the results by re-computing λ=(y2+y3)/(x2−x3)\lambda=(y_{2}+y_{3})/(x_{2}-x_{3}). This implies another exceptional case coming from the condition x3=x2x_{3}=x_{2}. Note that Roetteler et al. missed this fourth exceptional case in their analysis of the exceptional case count in [69, Section 4.2].

B.2 Approximate modular arithmetic failures

The second category of failures occurs because the modular arithmetic operations that are used in the affine point addition circuit are approximate operations themselves [71]. Again, there exist inputs for which the circuits fail to produce the expected results.

The modular arithmetic circuits presented here make use of the special shape of the pseudo-Mersenne base field prime pp. Several simplifications make modular arithmetic circuits more efficient but possibly lead to failures. For example, integer comparison with pp for modular reduction is replaced by comparison of the most significant bits and the correction addition that depends on the outcome of the comparison truncates the carry propagation. These optimizations are applied to the modular reduction operations in modular addition, subtraction, doubling, and halving circuits [71]. Similarly, truncated comparisons during phase corrections after measurement-based carry uncomputation can lead to phase failures even if the resulting values are correct. Furthermore, Dialog-based in-place multiplication [45, 71] uses a non-worst-case bound for both the number of iterations and the register sizes used as the algorithm progresses [64]. We begin by discussing the optimizations in modular reduction.

B.2.1 Approximate modular reduction

An element in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} is usually represented by its unique representative in {0,1,…,p−1}\{0,1,\dots,p-1\} (which we call the least non-negative or canonical representative). Integer arithmetic operations on such representatives may lead to values outside that range and a modular reduction is applied to reduce such a value back to its canonical representation. For example, taking two input operands from 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and adding their standard integer representatives results in a value 0≤u<2​p−10\leq u<2p-1. Modular reduction then subtracts pp if u≥pu\geq p, which means umodp=uu\bmod p=u, if u<pu<p, and umodp=u−pu\bmod p=u-p if u≥pu\geq p. Thus, there are two computational components, namely, computing the integer comparison u<pu<p and depending on its outcome an integer subtraction u−pu-p.

We work in the specific setting of a pseudo-Mersenne prime pp of bitlength nn. Let c∈ℕc\in\mathbb{N} be odd, c≪2nc\ll 2^{n} such that p=2n−cp=2^{n}-c. That pp has nn bits implies 2​c≤2n2c\leq 2^{n}. For the curve 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1}, we have n=256n=256 and c=232+29+28+27+26+24+1=232+977c=2^{32}+2^{9}+2^{8}+2^{7}+2^{6}+2^{4}+1=2^{32}+977. Subtracting such a pp results in u−p=u−(2n−c)=u+c−2nu-p=u-(2^{n}-c)=u+c-2^{n} and can be implemented by computing the addition u+cu+c and discarding the (n+1)(n+1)-th bit. Note that, if u≥pu\geq p, then u+c≥2nu+c\geq 2^{n} and its (n+1)(n+1)-th bit is always 11.

The two optimizations above, which were also used in previous work [71], lead to approximate modular reduction circuits that we use in different situations in our circuits. First, the full integer comparison u<pu<p is replaced by a comparison u<2nu<2^{n}, which amounts to simply observing the (n+1)(n+1)-th bit of uu. Instead of computing the integer comparison into a result bit that acts as the control for the modular subtraction, the (n+1)(n+1)-th bit directly serves as the control bit. This operation differs from exact integer comparison if

u∈[p,2n).u\in[p,2^{n}).

This means that for cc of the possible results of an addition, the optimized reduction fails to produce a canonical representative. Note that the result can still be represented with nn bits and is correct modulo pp but is by pp larger than the canonical representative. This behavior does not necessarily lead to a direct arithmetic failure; however, it might lead to failure cases when the larger result is used in further computations. We therefore treat non-canonical representatives for outputs of any operation as a failure case.

Second, for the addition u+cu+c, we truncate carry propagation after κ≤n\kappa\leq n bits for c<2κc<2^{\kappa} as in [71]. This operation differs from exact addition with full carry propagation if the carry propagates further than κ\kappa bits, i.e.,

umod2κ∈[2κ−c,2κ).u\bmod 2^{\kappa}\in[2^{\kappa}-c,2^{\kappa}).

This failure case, where the result is wrong modulo pp, occurs for a proportion of c/2κc/2^{\kappa} of input values, in which case the result after reduction is 2κ2^{\kappa} smaller than the correct one.

Because of the simplified comparison and since our circuits work on nn-bit quantum registers, we allow intermediate values modulo pp to be represented by integers in [0,2n)[0,2^{n}). We assume throughout that 2​c≤2κ≤2n2c\leq 2^{\kappa}\leq 2^{n}. For a non-negative integer uu, define

qu\displaystyle q_{u} =⌊u/2n⌋,ru=u−qu​2n∈[0,2n),\displaystyle=\lfloor u/2^{n}\rfloor,\quad r_{u}=u-q_{u}2^{n}\in[0,2^{n}),
wu\displaystyle w_{u} ={1, if ​(rumod2κ)≥2κ−c,0, otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1,\text{ if }\ (r_{u}\bmod 2^{\kappa})\geq 2^{\kappa}-c,\\ 0,\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

If u∈[0,2n+1)u\in[0,2^{n+1}), qu∈{0,1}q_{u}\in\{0,1\} is a single bit and the approximate reduction as described above then returns

redκ​(u)=ru+qu​c−qu​wu​2κ,\mathrm{red}_{\kappa}(u)=r_{u}+q_{u}c-q_{u}w_{u}2^{\kappa},

where quq_{u} is the (n+1)(n+1)-th bit, the correction is triggered if it is 11, in which case cc is added to the first nn bits of uu and the result is 2κ2^{\kappa} smaller than the correct value if the carry when adding cc propagates out of the first κ\kappa bits. Since the (n+1)(n+1)-th bit was discarded and the carry never propagates beyond the κ\kappa-th bit, redκ​(u)∈[0,2n)\mathrm{red}_{\kappa}(u)\in[0,2^{n}). Using 2n≡cmodp2^{n}\equiv c\bmod p and taking modulo pp gives

redκ​(u)≡u−qu​wu​2κ(modp),\mathrm{red}_{\kappa}(u)\equiv u-q_{u}w_{u}2^{\kappa}\pmod{p}, (62)

which means that the approximate reduction redκ\mathrm{red}_{\kappa} returns a correct integer representative of uu if and only if either no correction occurs (qu=0q_{u}=0) or the carry from the addition of cc does not propagate beyond κ\kappa bits (wu=0w_{u}=0). The above two failure cases imply incorrect result values. Another type of failure leads to an incorrect phase.

B.2.2 Approximate phase repair

To uncompute certain bits that are computed in our circuits such as a carry bit bb depending on a register |x⟩\ket{x}, we use measurement in the XX basis, which changes the phase by a factor (−1)m​b(-1)^{mb}, where mm is the measurement outcome. This means that a phase correction is required if m=1m=1 and b=1b=1. Our circuits use approximate recomputation of the bit bb for example by truncating carry propagation or comparing only the higher order bits. If the approximation is incorrect, a phase failure occurs because the circuit fails to correct the phase flip.

We now proceed to deduce bounds on the failure probabilities for the various components in the approximate affine point addition circuit. We start with the simpler modular operations such as addition, subtraction, and negation, then discuss the modular subtraction of a square, and finally, the in-place modular division and multiplication circuits.

B.2.3 Addition, subtraction, and negation
Addition.

The modular addition circuit we use [71] is an approximation of the operation |u⟩​|v⟩↦|u⟩​|(u+v)modp⟩\ket{u}\ket{v}\mapsto\ket{u}\ket{(u+v)\bmod p}. The inputs u,v∈[0,p)u,v\in[0,p) are canonical integer representatives of finite field elements. Let s=u+v∈[0,2p−1)⊆[0,2n+1)s=u+v\in[0,2p-1)\subseteq[0,2^{n+1}) be their integer sum. The circuit applies the approximate reduction described above and returns

redκ​(s)=rs+qs​c−qs​ws​2κ=s−qs​p−qs​ws​2κ.\mathrm{red}_{\kappa}(s)=r_{s}+q_{s}c-q_{s}w_{s}2^{\kappa}=s-q_{s}p-q_{s}w_{s}2^{\kappa}.

The circuit can fail to produce the correct result value in two different ways due to the applied approximations. The first is a failure due to the simplified comparison, where the most significant bit serves directly as the comparison bit. If p≤s<2np\leq s<2^{n}, no correction is applied. The result is correct modulo pp but remains larger than pp.

The second failure occurs if the simplified comparison is correct, it causes a correction but the truncated carry propagation modifies the result because the carry propagates further than κ\kappa bits. This happens for qs​ws=1q_{s}w_{s}=1 and the result is 2κ2^{\kappa} too small.

To count failure pairs (u,v)∈[0,p)2(u,v)\in[0,p)^{2}, i.e., pairs that lead to the above two failures, fix an integer value s∈[p,2p−1)s\in[p,2p-1) (no failure occurs for s∈[0,p)s\in[0,p)). For such ss, the number of (u,v)(u,v) with sum s=u+vs=u+v is 2​p−1−s2p-1-s. Summing over all relevant values for ss that lead to a simplified comparison failure yields their overall number as

∑s=p2n−1(2​p−1−s)=c⁡(2​p−c−1)2.\sum_{s=p}^{2^{n}-1}(2p-1-s)=\frac{c(2p-c-1)}{2}.

Failures due to truncated carry propagation occur when qs​ws=1q_{s}w_{s}=1 and rsmod2κ∈[2κ−c,2κ)r_{s}\bmod 2^{\kappa}\in[2^{\kappa}-c,2^{\kappa}). The relevant sums are of the form s=2n+j​2κ−1−bs=2^{n}+j2^{\kappa}-1-b, 1≤j≤2n−κ−11\leq j\leq 2^{n-\kappa}-1, 0≤b<c0\leq b<c. This time, the number of pairs (u,v)∈[0,p)2(u,v)\in[0,p)^{2} satisfying u+v=su+v=s for fixed ss is 2​p−1−s=2n−2​c−j​2κ+b2p-1-s=2^{n}-2c-j2^{\kappa}+b, and again, summing over the relevant values yields their overall count as

∑j=12n−κ−1∑b=0c−1(2n−2​c−j​2κ+b)\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{2^{n-\kappa}-1}\sum_{b=0}^{c-1}\left(2^{n}-2c-j2^{\kappa}+b\right)
=(2n−κ−1)​c​(2n−2​c)−c​2κ​2n−κ2​(2n−κ−1)\displaystyle=(2^{n-\kappa}-1)c(2^{n}-2c)-c2^{\kappa}\frac{2^{n-\kappa}}{2}(2^{n-\kappa}-1)
+(2n−κ−1)​c⁡(c−1)2\displaystyle\qquad+(2^{n-\kappa}-1)\frac{c(c-1)}{2}
=c⁡(2n−κ−1)​2n−3​c−12=c⁡(2n−κ−1)​p−2​c−12.\displaystyle=c(2^{n-\kappa}-1)\frac{2^{n}-3c-1}{2}=c(2^{n-\kappa}-1)\frac{p-2c-1}{2}.

The two cases fall into disjoint events because for the first, the simplified comparison does not lead to a correction (qs=0q_{s}=0), whereas for the second, it does (qs=1q_{s}=1).

A third failure case is a (−1)(-1)-phase that is not corrected due to a failure in the approximate recomputation of the bit qsq_{s} after an XX-measurement. This can happen even if the value of the representative is correctly computed. We are only interested in this case because it is disjoint from the previous two, where all value failures have been accounted for. This means that ws=0w_{s}=0, i.e., redκ​(s)=s−qs​p=rs+qs​c\mathrm{red}_{\kappa}(s)=s-q_{s}p=r_{s}+q_{s}c and the reduction yields the canonical representative.

The bit qsq_{s} can be precisely recovered using the fact that qs=0q_{s}=0 if and only if redκ​(s)≥u\mathrm{red}_{\kappa}(s)\geq u. The comparison used here is approximate, only taking into account the δ\delta most significant bits of redκ​(s)\mathrm{red}_{\kappa}(s) and uu. For a uniform distribution of (u,v)∈𝔽p×𝔽p(u,v)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}, the failure probability due to simplified comparison, truncated carry propagation, or truncated phase correction is

Naddp2<cp+c2κ+1+1+c/p2δ+1.\frac{N_{\mathrm{add}}}{p^{2}}<\frac{c}{p}+\frac{c}{2^{\kappa+1}}+\frac{1+c/p}{2^{\delta+1}}.
Inputs during affine point addition.

Inputs to the approximate addition in our elliptic curve point addition are not uniform random but intermediate results of our elliptic curve point addition.

Let (k,l)(k,l) be a fixed pair of scalars and 0≤i≤2​L−10\leq i\leq 2L-1. Assume no failures in the circuit up to the ii-th point addition step. Let A=(x1,y1)A=(x_{1},y_{1}) be the accumulator point and T=(x2,y2)T=(x_{2},y_{2}) the ii-th lookup point. Approximate addition is used three times in the point addition circuit: to compute (x1−x2)+Rmodp(x_{1}-x_{2})+R\bmod p, 3​x2+(x1−x2+R)modp3x_{2}+(x_{1}-x_{2}+R)\bmod p, and (R+x2−x3)+(−R)modp(R+x_{2}-x_{3})+(-R)\bmod p, where RR is a uniform random mask sampled fresh for each point addition step.

Note that we sample a0∈ℤr∗a_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{*} uniformly at random for each run of the double-scalar multiplication, and μi∈ℤr∖{−j​2i​w:0≤j<2w}\mu_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{r}\setminus\{-j2^{iw}:0\leq j<2^{w}\} and R∈𝔽pR\in\mathbb{F}_{p} are uniform random samples independent of a0a_{0} and each other for the ii-th windowed point addition step. The sample space of triples (a0,μi,R)(a_{0},\mu_{i},R) has size (r−1)​(r−2w)​p(r-1)(r-2^{w})p.

Since we assume no failures up to this point, and with fixed previous random mask values, the map (a0,μi)↦(A,T)(a_{0},\mu_{i})\mapsto(A,T) is injective. We can thus count the number of triples that lead to a given pair of inputs as follows.

For an input (R,x1−x2)(R,x_{1}-x_{2}) to the first addition to be equal to a fixed pair (u,v)∈𝔽p×𝔽p(u,v)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}, it has to satisfy R=uR=u and x1−x2=vx_{1}-x_{2}=v, which gives pp possible triples. The two xx-coordinates belong to at most two elliptic curve points each, meaning there are at most 4​p4p pairs (A,T)(A,T) corresponding to the given addition input pair. The same bound holds for the third addition. For the addition with inputs 3​x23x_{2} and x1−x2+Rx_{1}-x_{2}+R, 3​x2=u3x_{2}=u fixes x2x_{2}, yielding at most two curve points. There are at most r−1r-1 possible points AA, each of which then fixes x1x_{1} and thus RR. This means that there are at most 2​(r−1)2(r-1) points per addition input.

Adding these three counts and multiplying their sum by the number of addition failure pairs NaddN_{\mathrm{add}} gives a bound on the number of triples (a0,μi,R)(a_{0},\mu_{i},R) leading to one of the two approximation failures. Dividing by the total number of triples yields an upper bound on the addition failure probability paddp_{\mathrm{add}} during a single elliptic curve point addition as

padd\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{add}} ≤(8​p+2​(r−1))​Naddp⁡(r−1)​(r−2w)≤10​Nadd(r−1)​(r−2w)\displaystyle\leq\frac{(8p+2(r-1))N_{\mathrm{add}}}{p(r-1)(r-2^{w})}\leq\frac{10N_{\mathrm{add}}}{(r-1)(r-2^{w})}

Note that we used r−1<pr-1<p, which is not necessarily true for a general elliptic curve, but holds for 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1}.

Let n,w,p,c,r,κ,δn,w,p,c,r,\kappa,\delta be the parameters as described in this section. Let a0a_{0}, μi\mu_{i}, and RR be the random mask values as above. The probability paddp_{\mathrm{add}} over random (a0,μi,R)(a_{0},\mu_{i},R) that either a simplified comparison failure or a carry propagation failure occurs during one of the three approximate additions in the ii-th point addition step is bounded by

padd<10⋅2n−1(r−1)​(r−2w)​(c⁡(1+p−2​c2κ)+p−c2δ).\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{add}}<\frac{10\cdot 2^{n-1}}{(r-1)(r-2^{w})}\left(c(1+\frac{p-2c}{2^{\kappa}})+\frac{p-c}{2^{\delta}}\right).

padd<1.7463⋅10−9≈2−29.0931<2−29.093.p_{\mathrm{add}}<1.7463\cdot 10^{-9}\approx 2^{-29.0931}<2^{-29.093}.
Subtraction.

Our modular subtraction circuit is an approximation of |u⟩​|v⟩↦|u⟩​|(v−u)modp⟩\ket{u}\ket{v}\mapsto\ket{u}\ket{(v-u)\bmod p} for u,v∈[0,p)u,v\in[0,p). It is computed using the approximate addition, braced by two modular complements that implement the operation |x⟩↦|p−1−x⟩\ket{x}\mapsto\ket{p-1-x}. More precisely, the circuit realizes

|u⟩​|v⟩\displaystyle\ket{u}\ket{v} ↦|u⟩​|p−1−v⟩\displaystyle\mapsto\ket{u}\ket{p-1-v}
↦|u⟩​|((p−1−v)+u)modp⟩\displaystyle\mapsto\ket{u}\ket{((p-1-v)+u)\bmod p}
↦|u⟩​|p−1−((p−1−v+u)modp)⟩\displaystyle\mapsto\ket{u}\ket{p-1-((p-1-v+u)\bmod p)}
=|u⟩​|(v−u)modp⟩.\displaystyle=\ket{u}\ket{(v-u)\bmod p}.

Since we already obtained a bound on the failure probability due to approximate addition, it remains to bound the failure probability due to the approximate modular complement. The operation |x⟩↦|p−1−x⟩\ket{x}\mapsto\ket{p-1-x} is implemented by a bitwise complement followed by a truncated κ\kappa-bit addition of 2κ−c2^{\kappa}-c. The same result could be computed by a truncated addition of cc to xx followed by a bitwise complement. Without failures, this computes the modular complement because p−1−x=2n−c−1−x=((2n−1)−x)−c=(2n−1)−(x+c)p-1-x=2^{n}-c-1-x=((2^{n}-1)-x)-c=(2^{n}-1)-(x+c), again using the pseudo-Mersenne shape of pp. The only additional source of failures is the truncated carry propagation leading to an incorrect value if xmod2κ≥2κ−cx\bmod 2^{\kappa}\geq 2^{\kappa}-c. Counting failure inputs similarly to the analogous case for the modular addition, we obtain the number of inputs leading to a complement failure as

Ncmpl=c⁡(2n−κ−1),N_{\mathrm{cmpl}}=c(2^{n-\kappa}-1),

which means that for a uniform input, the failure probability due to truncated carry propagation in the modular complement is Ncmpl/p<c/2κN_{\mathrm{cmpl}}/p<c/2^{\kappa}.

Inputs during affine point addition.

Like in the analysis of approximate addition, we fix scalars (k,l)(k,l) and 0≤i≤2​L−10\leq i\leq 2L-1. Approximate subtraction occurs four times, namely to compute x1−x2x_{1}-x_{2}, y1−y2y_{1}-y_{2}, (y3+y2)−y2(y_{3}+y_{2})-y_{2}, and (x2−x3)−x2(x_{2}-x_{3})-x_{2}.

We argue very similarly to the addition case. Given x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}, there are at most 22 elliptic curve points with each xx-coordinate, hence at most 44. For a pair of yy-coordinates, there can be 33 points each due to the corresponding xx-coordinate satisfying a cubic equation, at most 99 points in total. Again, due to bijections mapping the pairs of points before and after the point addition and pairs of values through the ideal subtraction, the same bounds apply to the last two calls as to the first two.

Hence, we can conclude that the probability psubp_{\mathrm{sub}} of modular subtraction approximation failures during a single elliptic-curve point addition is

psub\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{sub}} ≤(4+9+9+4)​Nsub(r−1)​(r−2w).\displaystyle\leq\frac{(4+9+9+4)N_{\mathrm{sub}}}{(r-1)(r-2^{w})}.

Here, Nsub≤Nadd+2​p​NcmplN_{\mathrm{sub}}\leq N_{\mathrm{add}}+2pN_{\mathrm{cmpl}} is the number of input pairs that lead to a failure in the approximate subtraction circuit.

psub\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{sub}} ≤135​padd+52​p​c​(2n−κ−1)(r−1)​(r−2w).\displaystyle\leq\frac{13}{5}p_{\mathrm{add}}+\frac{52pc(2^{n-\kappa}-1)}{(r-1)(r-2^{w})}.

psub<1.0593796008×10−8≈2−26.4922<2−26.492.p_{\mathrm{sub}}<1.0593796008\times 10^{-8}\approx 2^{-26.4922}<2^{-26.492}.
Negation.

Finally, we analyze an approximation to |u⟩↦|(−u)modp⟩\ket{u}\mapsto\ket{(-u)\bmod p}. Modular negation is computed by a bitwise complement, which gives 2n−1−u2^{n}-1-u and then we subtract c−1c-1 to obtain 2n−c−u=p−u2^{n}-c-u=p-u. The subtraction is approximate by truncating it to κ\kappa bits. This leads to an incorrect value if umod2κ≥2κ−c+1u\bmod 2^{\kappa}\geq 2^{\kappa}-c+1. The integer value p−up-u is the correct canonical representative of the modular negative of uu except if u=0u=0. Therefore, the circuit swaps the values of 00 and pp at the end, leaving all other values intact.

Again, we have two failure cases. The first is due to truncated subtraction of c−1c-1 to κ\kappa bits, happening if umod2κ≥2κ−c+1u\bmod 2^{\kappa}\geq 2^{\kappa}-c+1, and thus is induced by (2n−κ−1)​(c−1)(2^{n-\kappa}-1)(c-1) of the canonical inputs.

The second failure is due to a shortened comparison window for the swap of 00 and pp to the τ\tau most-significant bits of the register. The swap is triggered when all these bits equal the least-significant bit. The circuit assumes that κ≤n−τ\kappa\leq n-\tau and τ≥2\tau\geq 2, otherwise it computes exact negation. Clearly, this comparison implementation has false positives, namely on non-zero even integers that are smaller than 2n−τ2^{n-\tau} and on odd integers in [2n−2n−τ,p)[2^{n}-2^{n-\tau},p). The total number of these failure cases is

(2n−τ−1−1)+2n−τ−c−12=2n−τ−c+32.\left(2^{n-\tau-1}-1\right)+\frac{2^{n-\tau}-c-1}{2}=2^{n-\tau}-\frac{c+3}{2}.

However, we have already counted some of these as failure cases, namely those that have the form u=j​2κ+2κ−c+hu=j2^{\kappa}+2^{\kappa}-c+h, 0≤j<2n−κ−10\leq j<2^{n-\kappa}-1, 1≤h<c1\leq h<c which lead to an intended intermediate value (2n−κ−j−1)​2κ−h(2^{n-\kappa}-j-1)2^{\kappa}-h. Counting the blocks in these intervals, the overlap has size

(2n−τ−κ+1−1)​c−12.(2^{n-\tau-\kappa+1}-1)\frac{c-1}{2}.

Since a failure due to the truncated subtraction cannot be corrected by a short swap failure, the total number of failure inputs for approximate negation is

Nneg\displaystyle N_{\mathrm{neg}} =(2n−κ−1)​(c−1)+2n−τ−c+32\displaystyle=(2^{n-\kappa}-1)(c-1)+2^{n-\tau}-\frac{c+3}{2}
−(2n−τ−κ+1−1)​c−12\displaystyle\qquad-(2^{n-\tau-\kappa+1}-1)\frac{c-1}{2}
=2n−τ+(c−1)​(2n−κ−2n−τ−κ)−c−1,\displaystyle=2^{n-\tau}+(c-1)(2^{n-\kappa}-2^{n-\tau-\kappa})-c-1,

which means that the failure probability for uniform input satisfies

Nnegp<c−12κ+1+c/p2τ.\frac{N_{\mathrm{neg}}}{p}<\frac{c-1}{2^{\kappa}}+\frac{1+c/p}{2^{\tau}}.
Inputs during affine point addition.

Modular negation occurs once to compute −x3modp-x_{3}\bmod p. Fixing an input uu therefore fixes x3x_{3}, so there are at most 22 elliptic curve points leading to this xx-coordinate. The table lookup point still can assume any of its r−2wr-2^{w} possible values, leading to 2​(r−2w)2(r-2^{w}) possible curve points leading to input x3x_{3}. With (r−1)​(r−2w)(r-1)(r-2^{w}) possible point pairs, the probability pnegp_{\mathrm{neg}} of a failure due to approximate negation during a single elliptic-curve point addition therefore is bounded by

pneg≤2​Nnegr−1.p_{\mathrm{neg}}\leq\frac{2N_{\mathrm{neg}}}{r-1}.

Let n,w,p,c,r,κn,w,p,c,r,\kappa be the parameters as described in this section. Let a0a_{0} and μi\mu_{i} be the random mask values as above. The probability pnegp_{\mathrm{neg}} over random (a0,μi)(a_{0},\mu_{i}) that either a truncated subtraction failure or a shortened comparison failure occurs during the approximate negation in the ii-th point addition step is bounded by
