pneg<6.9850⋅10−10≈2−30.4150<2−30.415.p_{\mathrm{neg}}<6.9850\cdot 10^{-10}\approx 2^{-30.4150}<2^{-30.415}.
B.2.4 Subtracting a square

Consider the subtraction of a square as described in Section VII. It acts on two registers and subtracts the square of the value in the first from that in the second modulo pp. It maps |x⟩​|y⟩\ket{x}\ket{y} to |x⟩​|(y−x2)modp⟩\ket{x}\ket{(y-x^{2})\bmod p}. We use a uniform random mask R∈𝔽pR\in\mathbb{F}_{p} that is added to the target register, which also acts as the accumulator register in the algorithm. The square subtraction circuit then maps

|x⟩​|(y+R)modp⟩↦|x⟩​|(y−x2+R)modp⟩\ket{x}\ket{(y+R)\bmod p}\mapsto\ket{x}\ket{(y-x^{2}+R)\bmod p}

and a subtraction of RR in the second register gives the desired result.

To understand the possible failure cases due to approximate arithmetic, we discuss the specific components as shown in Appendix A. The main operation is detailed for its integer-valued representation in Algorithm 6. It uses the components 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖡𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝖾±q\mathsf{AddBMultiple}_{\pm}^{q} (Algorithm 9), 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖢𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝖾−q\mathsf{AddCMultiple}_{-}^{q} (Algorithm 10), 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾σq\mathsf{AddSlice}_{\sigma}^{q} (Algorithm 7), and 𝖯𝗁𝖺𝗌𝖾𝖦𝖤q\mathsf{PhaseGE}^{q} (Algorithm 8). Notation and parameter properties are introduced in Appendix A.

Approximation failures in 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice}.

The basic component used in the other algorithms is 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} (Algorithm 7). It operates on two quantum registers, a source register and a target register, holding values ss and vv. It updates the target by adding σ2ts[o,o+w)\sigma 2^{t}s_{[o,o+w)}. The parameter δ\delta provides a way to trade efficiency for accuracy: it determines the number of bits used in the phase comparison, while the parameter ρ∈ℤ≥0\rho\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} is the carry-padding width for local slice additions. The parameters must satisfy either t+w+ρ<nt+w+\rho<n or t+w=nt+w=n with δ≤w\delta\leq w. There are four possible sources of approximation failures in 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice}.

A failure can occur during the complement computation of (p−1)−v(p-1)-v in the case of negative sign σ=−1\sigma=-1. While the bitwise complement operation is exact, the preceding addition of cc may drop a propagating carry. The corresponding failure preimage set is

E~compl={v∈[0,2n)∣v[0,κ)≥2κ−c}\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{compl}}=\{v\in[0,2^{n})\mid v_{[0,\kappa)}\geq 2^{\kappa}-c\}

and has cardinality c​ 2n−κc\,2^{n-\kappa}. Complement computation only happens if σ=−1\sigma=-1, but then it occurs twice, once when entering and once when leaving the complemented representation.

Another failure occurs for t+w+ρ<nt+w+\rho<n if in the addition of the source slice s′=s[o,o+w)s^{\prime}=s_{[o,o+w)} into vv, the carry propagates more than w+ρw+\rho bits. The failure preimage set is

E~carry(s,o,t,w)={v∈[0,2n)∣v[t,t+w+ρ)≥2w+ρ−s′}\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{carry}}(s,o,t,w)=\left\{v\in[0,2^{n})\mid v_{[t,t+w+\rho)}\geq 2^{w+\rho}-s^{\prime}\right\}

with cardinality s′​2n−w−ρ≤(2w−1)​2n−w−ρ<2n−ρs^{\prime}2^{n-w-\rho}\leq(2^{w}-1)2^{n-w-\rho}<2^{n-\rho}.

If t+w=nt+w=n, a carry that propagates more than ww bits means that the sum is at least 2n2^{n}. This carry is captured in an additional qubit, and an approximate reduction modulo pp is applied by adding cc with carry propagation truncated to κ\kappa bits. This failure case is captured by

E~wrap(s,o,t,w)={\displaystyle\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{wrap}}(s,o,t,w)=\{ v<2n|v+2t​s′≥2n,\displaystyle v<2^{n}\ \mid v+2^{t}s^{\prime}\geq 2^{n},
((v+2ts′)mod2n)[0,κ)≥2κ−c}.\displaystyle((v+2^{t}s^{\prime})\bmod 2^{n})_{[0,\kappa)}\geq 2^{\kappa}-c\}.

Translation by 2ts[o,o+w)2^{t}s_{[o,o+w)} modulo 2n2^{n} is a bijection. Dropping the carry condition therefore upper bounds the cardinality of this set by the usual truncated carry-propagation bound c​2n−κc2^{n-\kappa}.

The fourth failure case in 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} is a failure due to an approximate phase correction in the case t+w=nt+w=n. The extra carry bit can be uncomputed by an XX-measurement and phase correction. Let h=𝟙[v+2ts[o,o+w)≥2n]h=\mathbbm{1}[v+2^{t}s_{[o,o+w)}\geq 2^{n}] and

v+=((v+2ts[o,o+w))mod2n)+hc.v^{+}=((v+2^{t}s_{[o,o+w)})\bmod 2^{n})+hc.

If no failure occurs due to E~wrap​(s,o,t,w)\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{wrap}}(s,o,t,w), the addition of h​chc has no carry out of the low κ\kappa bits, so v+<2nv^{+}<2^{n}. When m=1m=1 is measured, the exact carry correction contributes the phase (−1)q(-1)^{q}. Together with a full-width call to 𝖯𝗁𝖺𝗌𝖾𝖦𝖤\mathsf{PhaseGE}, it gives

(−1)q(−1)q𝟙[(v+)[t,n)≥s[o,o+w)]=(−1)q𝟙[(v+)[t,n)<s[o,o+w)],(-1)^{q}(-1)^{q\mathbbm{1}[(v^{+})_{[t,n)}\geq s_{[o,o+w)}]}=(-1)^{q\mathbbm{1}[(v^{+})_{[t,n)}<s_{[o,o+w)}]},

The implementation supplies only the most-significant δ\delta bits to 𝖯𝗁𝖺𝗌𝖾𝖦𝖤\mathsf{PhaseGE}, and the resulting reconstruction can fail for two reasons. First, when h=1h=1, the corresponding full-width comparison reconstructs hh exactly if and only if v<pv<p; hence a non-canonical input v≥pv\geq p causes a failure. Second, the comparison on the most-significant δ\delta bits can disagree with the full-width comparison. The failure preimage sets for those events are

E~ph,rep(s,o,t,w)={v∈[0,2n)|v≥p,h=1},\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{ph,rep}}(s,o,t,w)=\left\{v\in[0,2^{n})\ \middle|\ v\geq p,\quad h=1\right\},

with cardinality at most cc and (with s′=s[o,o+w)s^{\prime}=s_{[o,o+w)})

E~ph,trunc(s,o,t,w)={\displaystyle\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{ph,trunc}}(s,o,t,w)=\{ v<2n∣𝟙[(v+)[t,n)≥s′]\displaystyle v<2^{n}\ \mid\mathbbm{1}[(v^{+})_{[t,n)}\geq s^{\prime}]
≠𝟙[(v+)[n−δ,n)≥s[w−δ,w)′]},\displaystyle\neq\mathbbm{1}[(v^{+})_{[n-\delta,n)}\geq s^{\prime}_{[w-\delta,w)}]\},

and |E~ph,trunc​(s,o,t,w)|≤2n−δ|\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{ph,trunc}}(s,o,t,w)|\leq 2^{n-\delta}. The bound on the second cardinality follows because if the two comparisons disagree, the δ\delta most significant bits of the values must be equal, fixing δ\delta of the bits of v+v^{+}.

The operation 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖢𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝖾\mathsf{AddCMultiple} adds or subtracts a multiple of cc using the signed binary representation list TcT_{c}. For 0≤s<2n0\leq s<2^{n}, each element in TcT_{c} with d>0d>0 satisfies 2ds=2ds[0,n−d)+2ns[n−d,n)2^{d}s=2^{d}s_{[0,n-d)}+2^{n}s_{[n-d,n)}; if d=0d=0, there is no decomposition. The decomposition into low and high parts at the boundary nn allows the addition of the high parts to be postponed and later corrected by combining them into hs=∑(d,ϵ)∈Tcϵs[n−d,n)h_{s}=\sum_{(d,\epsilon)\in T_{c}}\epsilon s_{[n-d,n)}. This contributes 2n​hs≡c​hs(modp)2^{n}h_{s}\equiv ch_{s}\pmod{p}. For 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1}, where n=256n=256, this is

hs=s[224,256)+s[246,256)−s[250,256)+s[252,256),h_{s}=s_{[224,256)}+s_{[246,256)}-s_{[250,256)}+s_{[252,256)},

and 0≤hs≤c−30\leq h_{s}\leq c-3. Hence 0≤c​hs<2650\leq ch_{s}<2^{65}, so the high correction fits in the fixed 65-bit auxiliary register. The implementation constructs c​hsch_{s} by exact reversible signed additions modulo 2652^{65}. Intermediate values may get reduced modulo 2652^{65}, but the final residue is the ordinary integer c​hsch_{s}. Reversing the same sequence therefore clears the auxiliary qubits. 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖢𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝖾\mathsf{AddCMultiple} makes five calls to 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} for the direct shifted terms and one call for the high correction c​hsch_{s}. The exact construction and uncomputation of c​hsch_{s} introduce no additional target-dependent failure sites, so all such sites occur in these six calls to 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice}.

For 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷\mathtt{secp256k1}, the square-subtract trace contains three calls to 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖡𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝖾\mathsf{AddBMultiple}, each containing one call to 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} with three wrapping sites and five 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} calls with three occurrences of the local carry failure sites. There is one call to the negative version of 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖢𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝖾\mathsf{AddCMultiple}, which has five 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} calls that can wrap and one local call for the upper bits correction. The negative terms in the representation of cc contribute ten complement failure sites and five phase corrections. Overall, there are 1616 local 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} calls, 99 wrapping calls, and 1313 negative calls, giving 2626 complement sites.

Intermediate results in the algorithm can lie in [0,2n)[0,2^{n}) and thus be non-canonical representations of elements modulo pp. However, under a failure-free execution on canonical inputs, the outputs lie again in [0,p)[0,p) and are thus canonical. This is clear if the control is q=0q=0 as the operation is the identity. For q=1q=1, the last operation of the algorithm that acts on the output register is a modular complement implemented by an addition of cc followed by a bitwise complement in the last line of the 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{AddSlice} algorithm, which is called with negative sign σ=−1\sigma=-1 from 𝖠𝖽𝖽𝖡𝖬𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗂𝗉𝗅𝖾\mathsf{AddBMultiple}. On a failure-free execution, the truncated addition of cc into the vv register right before the complement succeeds, which means that vmod2κ<2κ−cv\bmod 2^{\kappa}<2^{\kappa}-c because no carry has propagated out of the lowest κ\kappa bits. Since v<2nv<2^{n}, we have v+c<2nv+c<2^{n}, thus v<pv<p and the bitwise complement correctly computes (2n−1)−(v+c)=p−1−v∈[0,p)(2^{n}-1)-(v+c)=p-1-v\in[0,p). Therefore, any failure that would lead to a non-canonical output is already accounted for through previous failures.

Overall, under the helper conditions above, and assuming a uniformly masked target and exact integer squaring operations, residue projection and a union bound give bounds for the probabilities pvalp_{\mathrm{val}} of complement, wrapping and carry failures and pphasep_{\mathrm{phase}} of phase correction errors as

pval\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{val}} ≤(1+cp)​(162ρ+35​c2κ),\displaystyle\leq\left(1+\frac{c}{p}\right)\left(\frac{16}{2^{\rho}}+\frac{35c}{2^{\kappa}}\right),
pphase\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{phase}} ≤(1+cp)​(92δ+9​c2256).\displaystyle\leq\left(1+\frac{c}{p}\right)\left(\frac{9}{2^{\delta}}+\frac{9c}{2^{256}}\right).

Consequently, the coherent failure probability psqp_{\mathrm{sq}} for the square-subtract operation satisfies

psq≤(1+cp)​(162ρ+35​c2κ+92δ+9​c2256).\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{sq}}\leq\left(1+\frac{c}{p}\right)\left(\frac{16}{2^{\rho}}+\frac{35c}{2^{\kappa}}+\frac{9}{2^{\delta}}+\frac{9c}{2^{256}}\right).

For ρ=δ=32\rho=\delta=32 and κ=65\kappa=65, this gives psq<2−26.59p_{\mathrm{sq}}<2^{-26.59}.

B.2.5 Approximate in-place multiplication and division

Another component needed in the point addition circuit is an in-place modular multiplication and its inverse, which functions as an in-place modular division, as described in Schrottenloher’s recent work [71]. It is used to compute and uncompute the slope λ\lambda. While we have proved failure bounds for the modular squaring operation and the coordinate offset computations in the previous section, we obtain a bound on the failure probability for the gcd-based in-place multiplication by a Monte Carlo simulation instead. We sampled 1,000,0001{,}000{,}000 uniformly random pairs (u,v)∈𝔽p∗×𝔽p(u,v)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}, simulated our approximate circuits to compute |u⟩​|v⟩↦|u⟩​|(u​v)modp⟩\ket{u}\ket{v}\mapsto\ket{u}\ket{(uv)\bmod p} and |u⟩​|v⟩↦|u⟩​|(u−1​v)modp⟩\ket{u}\ket{v}\mapsto\ket{u}\ket{(u^{-1}v)\bmod p}, and counted the number of inputs for which the circuit failed (wrong output, residual phase, deallocation of a nonzero ancilla, etc.). The simulation recorded K=21K=21 failures for both operations. The circuit parameters we used were mostly identical to the ones used by Schrottenloher [71]. We list the parameters in Table 10.

The simulation allows us to make the following statement using the Clopper-Pearson [18] bound: With confidence level at least 1−2−1291-2^{-129}, the probability that the in-place multiplication procedure using the binary gcd algorithm with the above parameters fails under uniform random inputs (u,v)∈𝔽p∗×𝔽p(u,v)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}\times\mathbb{F}_{p} is bounded by 0.0001493040.000149304. In turn, this allows us to conclude via union bound that with confidence level at least 1−2−1281-2^{-128}, both in-place multiplications succeed with probability at least 1−2⋅0.0001493041-2\cdot 0.000149304 for uniform random inputs from 𝔽p∗×𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}.

Since the actual inputs to the in-place multiplication in the circuit are differences of elliptic curve point coordinates, their distribution is not equal to the uniform distribution used in the simulation. This introduces a factor of approximately 44 into the bound inequality, which we will show next.

The actual input to the first in-place modular division algorithm is the pair of differences (x1−x2,y1−y2)(x_{1}-x_{2},y_{1}-y_{2}). Here Ai=(x1,y1)A_{i}=(x_{1},y_{1}) is the current accumulator point after ii point addition steps, i.e., Ai=(x1,y1)=A0+SiA_{i}=(x_{1},y_{1})=A_{0}+S_{i}, where SiS_{i} is the point accumulated into A0A_{0} after ii steps. The point (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) is the point looked up in the ii-th window from the ii-th lookup table TiT_{i}.

Because a0←$ℤr∗a_{0}\xleftarrow{\$}\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{*} is sampled uniformly at random and the map A0↦AiA_{0}\mapsto A_{i} as a shift by the point SiS_{i} is injective, and we only need to take into account first-time failures of trajectories that are correct up to this point, the point AiA_{i} can be one of r−1r-1 points, namely in the set E⁡(𝔽p)∖{𝒪}+SiE(\mathbb{F}_{p})\setminus\{\mathcal{O}\}+S_{i}.

The point (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) is of the form [j​2i​w+μi]​P[j2^{iw}+\mu_{i}]P or [j​2(i−L)​w+μi]​Q[j2^{(i-L)w}+\mu_{i}]Q. Since μi\mu_{i} is sampled uniformly at random from ℤr∖{−2i​w​j∣j∈{0,1,…,2w−1}}\mathbb{Z}_{r}\setminus\{-2^{iw}j\mid j\in\{0,1,\dots,2^{w}-1\}\} or ℤr∖{−2(i−L)​w​j∣j∈{0,1,…,2w−1}}\mathbb{Z}_{r}\setminus\{-2^{(i-L)w}j\mid j\in\{0,1,\dots,2^{w}-1\}\}, the point can be any point in E⁡(𝔽p)E(\mathbb{F}_{p}) except for the set of points of size 2w2^{w} given by the exceptions above.

B.4 Algorithm success probability with approximate arithmetic

In this section, we derive a bound on the success probability of Shor’s algorithm for solving the ECDLP when using approximate double scalar multiplication with failure bound pfp_{f}. Our bound takes into account wrong outputs as well as phase errors due to approximate phase-fix predicates.

Recall the failure set

Bω={(k,l)∈\displaystyle B_{\omega}=\{(k,l)\in [0,2n)×[0,2n)∣\displaystyle[0,2^{n})\times[0,2^{n})\mid
fω(k,l)≠f~ω(k,l)∨sω(k,l)=−1}\displaystyle f_{\omega}(k,l)\neq\widetilde{f}_{\omega}(k,l)\vee s_{\omega}(k,l)=-1\}

for the masked approximate implementation f~ω​(k,l)\tilde{f}_{\omega}(k,l), i.e., the set of inputs (k,l)(k,l) for which the masked approximate implementation does not agree with the ideal masked value fω​(k,l)f_{\omega}(k,l) or it agrees but the implementation produces a residual (−1)(-1)-phase.

For the analysis, we assume that we perform the known translation from fω​(k,l)f_{\omega}(k,l) to f⁡(k,l)f(k,l) right after applying the oracle, i.e., we assume that the random point offsets of the masked implementation are removed. Because the projector onto successful outcomes of the algorithm (see the definition of MM below) only acts on the input register, this shift does not affect outcome probabilities, and thus does not have to be implemented in practice. However, this assumption simplifies the analysis significantly. For brevity, we will write x∈X:=[0,2n)×[0,2n)x\in X:=[0,2^{n})\times[0,2^{n}) instead of (k,l)(k,l) and f⁡(x)f(x) instead of f⁡(k,l)f(k,l).

Let N=22​n=|X|N=2^{2n}=|X| and the ideal state before the QFT-measurement

|Ψ⟩=1N​∑x∈X|x⟩​|f⁡(x)⟩.\ket{\Psi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{x\in X}\ket{x}\ket{f(x)}.

The corresponding approximate state is

Appendix C End-to-end integrated routing

Appendix D Circuit synthesis

Circuit synthesis turns the verified hierarchy of specs and defs into an architecture-legal, executable schedule. The entry point takes a root spec and its parameters, a target architecture, an optional layout plan, and synthesis options; it returns the measurement schedule together with its metrics and a serialized schedule artifact from which all downstream reporting is derived.

The architecture object declares a group of memory blocks and one or more groups of factory blocks. The memory type fixes block size and shape, which operations are directly legal within one block or between two blocks, and how many concurrent operations and logical measurements a block supports. Each factory group names a resource-state kind, a block count, the number of states per block, and the preparation and cleanup recipes for that factory type—for the ECC pipeline, CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} factories. Legality checks, placement, and resource allocation all key off this object.

D.1 Synthesis tree and frontier lowering

Synthesis expands the root into a synthesis tree that records the decomposing hierarchy, the def selected at each node, qubit and classical-bit bindings, and classical conditions on components. The frontier lowering loop repeatedly selects a frontier node, chooses a def if the node is not directly legal on the architecture, allocates and binds the def’s ancillae, and expands the node—until every leaf is architecture-legal. Routing is handled by placement and by local measurement-based gadgets rather than a separate global SWAP\mathrm{SWAP} network: an operation that is not legal in the current geometry is decomposed into components such as logical measurements, controlled loads, CNOT\mathrm{CNOT} fanout, or PcP gadgets (though we managed to entirely avoid naively decomposing PcPs in this work).

Schedule-dependent resource binding is deferred during this refinement: factory ancillae are virtual qubits in the tree, so defs and legality checks remain coherent while the physical factory assignment is chosen later, at scheduling time. Run-local facts—qubit ownership, ordering dependencies—are recorded in synthesis-side state and never leak into the reusable specs and defs. Two further mechanisms keep synthesis tractable at application scale: a compact representation of repeated structure, and memoized replay of previously lowered subtrees.

D.2 Compact repetition and deferred parameters

Repeated algorithmic structure is kept as a compact repeated subcircuit rather than expanded into a separate copy for every iteration. Its compile-time bounds determine how many times the body executes, while an iteration variable may select the operand qubit, register slice, constant, or implementation variant used on each pass. Repetitions may be nested or traversed in reverse, and inverting a repeated computation reverses both the iteration order and the enclosed operations. This representation is used for repeated shifts, multiplier digit sweeps, lookup traversal, modular-inversion rounds, and the repeated work units above point addition.

The repeated body remains compact while the compiler selects implementations, checks architectural legality, estimates costs, and records the synthesis state. When different iterations genuinely require different circuit shapes, the alternatives are selected by the iteration variable; changing register widths are a common example. Only when the final operation stream is emitted does the compiler substitute concrete operands and iteration-local classical results for every pass. This late expansion reduces compilation work and memory even though the executable schedule ultimately contains every operation.

D.3 Memoized lowering and subtree replay

The second mechanism is a dynamic-programming-style replay cache. After a subtree has been lowered completely, the compiler records its expansion under a structural key containing the source spec type and normalized parameters, the chosen def, and compatible ancilla bindings. These immutable tuples are hashable, so a repeated semantic component can locate an earlier lowering with a dictionary lookup rather than repeating recursive def selection, child-support tests, allotment, and layout decisions. Separate run-local caches remember preferred defs and architecture-support results.

On a replay hit, the compiler reproduces the cached child structure under the new occurrence and remaps occurrence-local classical identities. The replayed state includes the selected decomposition, ancilla bindings, sibling topology, factory-loan annotations, and qubit-ownership classes; it is not merely a copy of a flattened gate string. A candidate is rejected when its completed subtree or resource context is not safe to reuse, in which case ordinary expansion is performed. Rewinding or editing the live tree invalidates the affected cached state. These restrictions make hashing an optimization only: enabling or disabling replay must not change the emitted program.

This reuse happens during hierarchical synthesis, before measurement scheduling: the scheduler receives the bound serial stream and constructs concrete layers for every occurrence, so the replay speedup is a lowering speedup. Scheduler-side scalability comes instead from the packed layer representation and the optional late resolution of classical conditions described next.

D.4 Measurement scheduling

Beyond the general routine described in the main text, the scheduler applies a resource-pool model to state injections. Each CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} factory use is split into an injection (three Z​ZZZ logical measurements, each coupling one CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} state qubit to its memory target) and factory cleanup measurements. The scheduler tracks the number of available resource states per factory kind, decrementing on injection and incrementing on cleanup, and when a cleanup is delayed the propagating phase fix is tracked as a conditional Pauli byproduct. Only after scheduling are virtual factory indices assigned to physical factory blocks, pairing each injection with its matching cleanup. Internally, layers are stored as block-local Pauli bitmasks and flat instruction buffers rather than per-gate objects—the representation change that makes scheduling application-scale circuits tractable.

D.5 Layout plans

A layout plan is an authored, scoped placement policy for one spec implementation. It can force the def choice for its spec (and, through nested child plans, for the children) and binds semantic ports and ancillae to placement rules: serial strips through memory blocks, interleaved cycles, or direct block-and-slot coordinates. It can also reserve pools of helper qubits for Pauli-controlled-Pauli (PcP) gadgets. The plan is where design-level decisions enter: which registers are colocated, which resource pools exist, and which defs are forced. Below the planned shape the compiler still applies its local policies, but changing the plan changes the compiled tree, the schedule pressure, and the resulting metrics.

Appendix E Architecture resource totals

The compiled-circuit resource counts used throughout this section are summarized in Table 11.

We note that the total number of Toffoli injections is different from the reported estimate in Part III, where we used the accounting from previous work.

This is for three reasons: (1) as discussed in Sec. X, we always execute conditional phase comparators in our compiled circuits as opposed to only counting operations if they are executed (as in previous work [3, 71]); (2) our phase-fix lookup is implemented suboptimally, i.e., we have not implemented the phaseup operation from [31]; and (3) the counts in Table 11 include the initial lookup replacing the first point addition.

Algorithm-wide exhaustion budget.

For a reservoir of capacity rr, we call the period between consecutive reservoir refills a refill interval, and let XX be the number of replacement ions demanded during that interval. We define exhaustion as the event X>rX>r, in which the replacement demand exceeds the available stock before the next refill. We assume that exhaustion of any local or global reservoir counts as a failed run and choose the reservoir capacities to bound the total run-wide exhaustion probability below the target

εres=10−3.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{res}}=10^{-3}. (64)

Meeting this target ensures that reservoir exhaustion contributes at most 0.10.1 percentage points to the failure probability of an attempt.

Cat-state bundle pairs and Bell-state resources.

Let kcatk_{\mathrm{cat}} denote the maximum number of logical measurements that the device must support in parallel. The reuse schedule of Sec. XII.3.2 assigns two mobile cat-state bundles to each measurement stream. For Q102, each bundle contains one weight-3030 cat-state register and one weight-3030 verification bank; the weight 3030 is set by the widest logical measurement made in a Q102 block. Together, the two bundles allocated to one measurement stream form a cat-state bundle pair. Each bundle occupies 2×30=602\times 30=60 physical qubits, so each bundle pair occupies 120120 physical qubits. The resulting footprint is therefore

nphyscat​(kcat)=2​kcat​(2×30)=120​kcat.n_{\mathrm{phys}}^{\mathrm{cat}}(k_{\mathrm{cat}})=2k_{\mathrm{cat}}(2\times 30)=120k_{\mathrm{cat}}. (79)

nphyscat=120​kcat(peak)=120​(24)=2,880.n_{\mathrm{phys}}^{\mathrm{cat}}=120k_{\mathrm{cat}}^{(\mathrm{peak})}=120(24)=2{,}880. (80)

In each cat-state production round, every LM2 measurement involving memory blocks consumes kBellk_{\mathrm{Bell}} Bell pairs to stitch the two cat states used in that round, where kBellk_{\mathrm{Bell}} is the number of pairs required to verify the stitched cat state with undetected-error probability at most ε\varepsilon. Following the Walking Cat stitching protocol [78], each Bell pair is prepared with a small unitary circuit. One qubit from each pair is routed to each of the two target cat-state factories. At the two factories, we measure a joint Z​ZZZ-stabilizer parity check between each Bell-pair qubit and one qubit of the local cat state. This procedure stitches the two cat states into a larger, joint cat state. Each Bell pair supplies one stabilizer measurement of the joint cat state, so the kBellk_{\mathrm{Bell}} pairs provide kBellk_{\mathrm{Bell}} redundant stitch checks. Writing p′≤4​pp^{\prime}\leq 4p for the error rate of one stitch check, including Bell-pair and transport faults, an incorrect parity can induce a high-weight XX error on one half of the stitched cat state, but the stitch is rejected unless all kBellk_{\mathrm{Bell}} stitch checks return the same wrong value. At p=10−4p=10^{-4}, choosing kBell=4k_{\mathrm{Bell}}=4 gives (p′)kBell≤(4​p)4=2.56×10−14(p^{\prime})^{k_{\mathrm{Bell}}}\leq(4p)^{4}=2.56\times 10^{-14}, below the target precision ε=10−11\varepsilon=10^{-11}. We provision one Bell-state bundle for each of the 12 simultaneous LM2 measurements at peak demand. Each bundle therefore contains 2​kBell=82k_{\mathrm{Bell}}=8 physical qubits, including while those qubits are in flight. The four independent pairs can be prepared in parallel in two POCs, well within the 13.45–14.8-POC cat-state production interval; we assume that pre-positioning the bundles similarly hides their transport latency, so no additional Bell pairs are required for pipelining. E.2 Runtime

The compiled algorithm has measurement-layer depth Dmeas=75,251,329D_{\mathrm{meas}}=75{,}251{,}329, as listed in Table 11. To obtain an upper bound on the runtime, we assign every measurement layer the mean duration of a CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection. Among the logical measurements used in the compiled elliptic-curve point-addition circuits, a CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection has the longest mean duration. It also determines the critical path whenever it appears in a parallel layer, because its outcome is needed to resolve subsequent Clifford corrections on the data blocks. The three independent Viterbi processes in a CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} injection have a joint average stopping time of 5.465.46 Q102 SECs, as derived in eq. 26. Since one Q102 SEC takes 27 POCs, this gives Tinj=147.48T_{\mathrm{inj}}=147.48 POCs, or approximately 0.029500.02950 seconds, when evaluated using the unrounded duration. The resulting expected-runtime upper bound per attempt is therefore

Trun\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{run}} ≲Dmeas×0.0294958​s\displaystyle\lesssim D_{\mathrm{meas}}\times 0.0294958~\mathrm{s}
=75,251,329×0.0294958​s\displaystyle=75{,}251{,}329\times 0.0294958~\mathrm{s}
=2,219,600​s≈25.7​days.\displaystyle=2{,}219{,}600~\mathrm{s}\approx 25.7~\mathrm{days}. (85)

E.3 Logical failure probability

We include five contributions to the algorithm-wide logical failure probability: memory errors in the Q102 blocks, errors in logical measurements, errors in the CCZ\mathrm{CCZ} states consumed by Toffoli gates, errors in the TT states consumed by the iQFT, and reservoir exhaustion.

Memory errors.

As an upper bound, we assume that all Dmeas=75,251,329D_{\mathrm{meas}}=75{,}251{,}329 measurement layers occur on all 6969 Q102 memory blocks in the device. But, in actuality, only a small subset of qubits needs to hold quantum information continuously for this whole time in the application, so our upper bound is quite conservative. We find

NSEC\displaystyle N_{\mathrm{SEC}} =Dmeas×τCCZavg×69\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{meas}}\times\tau_{\mathrm{CCZ}}^{\mathrm{avg}}\times 69
=75,251,329×τCCZavg×69\displaystyle=75{,}251{,}329\times\tau_{\mathrm{CCZ}}^{\mathrm{avg}}\times 69
=2.83615×1010.\displaystyle=2.83615\times 10^{10}. (86)

At the Q102 logical error rate pL,SECQ102=9.34×10−12p_{\mathrm{L,SEC}}^{\mathrm{Q102}}=9.34\times 10^{-12} per SEC from Table 4, this corresponds to a memory-failure probability of

pmem=1−(1−pL,SECQ102)NSEC=0.2327.p_{\mathrm{mem}}=1-\left(1-p_{\mathrm{L,SEC}}^{\mathrm{Q102}}\right)^{N_{\mathrm{SEC}}}=0.2327. (87)

The four Q102 logical CliNR blocks hold encoded states only for the duration of frame clearing, rather than for the full algorithm. Their exposure is therefore included in the non-Toffoli logical-measurement count below, not in the long-lived memory-failure total.

Although the calculated memory-failure probability is relatively high, our estimate is substantially inflated by the assumption that all 69 Q102 blocks continuously hold quantum information throughout the algorithm. The probability can also be readily reduced by increasing the code distance or tuning the decoder, as discussed for the memory-error bottleneck in the magic factory.

For a weight-3030 Viterbi measurement at physical error rate p=10−4p=10^{-4}, the single-round bit-flip model gives pflip,30=2.1×30×10−4=6.3×10−3p_{\mathrm{flip},30}=2.1\times 30\times 10^{-4}=6.3\times 10^{-3}. A vote margin of five therefore has logical error probability

pVit,30=[1+(1−pflip,30pflip,30)5]−1=1.02×10−11.p_{\mathrm{Vit},30}=\left[1+\left(\frac{1-p_{\mathrm{flip},30}}{p_{\mathrm{flip},30}}\right)^{5}\right]^{-1}=1.02\times 10^{-11}. (88)

For Nnon​-​Tof=369,882,166N_{\mathrm{non\text{-}Tof}}=369{,}882{,}166 such non-Toffoli logical measurements, as listed in Table 11, their combined failure probability is 1−(1−pVit,30)Nnon​-​Tof=0.003781-(1-p_{\mathrm{Vit},30})^{N_{\mathrm{non\text{-}Tof}}}=0.00378.

Eastinthillation factory errors.

The Eastinthillation factory has logical error rate pLCCZ≲9.36×10−10p_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{CCZ}}\lesssim 9.36\times 10^{-10} per accepted state from eq. 60. Using one accepted state for each of NTof=40,420,330N_{\mathrm{Tof}}=40{,}420{,}330 Toffoli injections from Table 11, the cumulative failure probability of the Eastinthillation factories is

pCCZ=1−(1−pLCCZ)NTof≲0.0371.p_{\mathrm{CCZ}}=1-\left(1-p_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{CCZ}}\right)^{N_{\mathrm{Tof}}}\lesssim 0.0371. (89)
iQFT-stage errors.

The 5,6845{,}684 accepted TT-state pairs and 464464 synthesized rotations used for the iQFT contribute

piQFT≤7.64×10−5,p_{\mathrm{iQFT}}\leq 7.64\times 10^{-5}, (90)

as calculated in eq. 61.

Reservoir exhaustion.

The device’s reservoir-exhaustion probability is at most 7.32×10−47.32\times 10^{-4}.

Assuming these five failure mechanisms are statistically independent, their contributions combine to give

pfail,alg\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{fail,alg}} ≤1−(1−0.2327)​(1−0.00378)\displaystyle\leq 1-(1-0.2327)(1-0.00378)
×(1−0.0371)​(1−7.64×10−5)\displaystyle\quad{}\times(1-0.0371)(1-7.64\times 10^{-5})
×(1−7.32×10−4)\displaystyle\quad{}\times(1-7.32\times 10^{-4})
=0.2646≈26%.\displaystyle=0.2646\approx 26\%. (91)

Appendix F Swap-loss sensitivity

We choose pswap=0.5p_{\mathrm{swap}}=0.5 as a conservative order-one swap probability. The precise choice has little effect on the reported logical error rate: with the swap-resilient LDU, the simulations show no discernible dependence on pswapp_{\mathrm{swap}} over the tested range [0,0.75][0,0.75], within statistical uncertainty, as shown in Fig. 23.
